ACM, New York, NY, USA, 7 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3724363.3729029 Group formation is an important issue in collaborative learning, as properly formed groups can lead to better interactions between students and enhance their learning. This issue also applies to pair programming when it is used as a learning activity. When the number of students is important and/or students and teachers do not know each other very well, manual group formation, either by students or teachers, can become difficult. Many of the existing automatic methods used for automatic group formation in pair programming require a certain amount of personal information about the students, which can make the implementation of this kind of system difficult. Hence, in this paper we present an automatic pair formation method integrated to a distributed pair programming application. Our approach is based on personal data from the students collected with questionnaires within our platform, but also on trace data automatically collected from the pair programming activities completed by students. It has been experimented during an introductory programming course in higher education. The objective was to identify, among programming experience, self-efficacy, gender and past engagement in pair programming activities, the formation criteria that led to the best perceived compatibility and work distribution as well as performance. The results show that homogeneous pairs in self-efficacy are significantly better than heterogeneous pairs, both in terms of perceived compatibility and perceived work distribution.

papers.title: FEEDBOT: Formative Design Feedback on Programming Assignments
papers.authors: Northeastern University Boston, Northeastern University Boston, Northeastern University Boston, Northeastern University Boston
papers.abstract: and provides limited but actionable hints. This approach preserves student agency by not revealing solutions. Briefly, the Design Recipe proceeds as follows: data design is accomplished by (1) identifying the values that make up the data, (2) describing (in a comment) how the data will be used in the program, (3) writing down examples of the data, and (4) constructing an example function "template" showing how the data might be used. Function design is done by (1) describing the input and output types of the function, (2) writing down a concise statement (in English) of what the function does, (3) writing example function uses (test cases), and (4) implementing the function. Since FEEDBOT knows whether a given problem is a data design problem or a function design problem, its task is to: (1) assess whether all four steps have been completed satisfactorily and if not, (2) identify the first step that needs work. Since the steps are intentionally sequential, the first step with issues is the ideal place for a student to begin improving their work. Additionally, since the steps are granular yet general, the mere identification of that step strikes a good balance of giving students guidance without giving them so much assistance that they do not learn from doing the work on their own. While FEEDBOT is not bound to the Design Recipe, its success is certainly due to the sequential and granular nature of this pedagogical framework, and likely without it the tool would have similar struggles to other tools in this space. This paper describes FEEDBOT, an open-source formative assessment tool leveraging large language models (LLMs) to provide structured, high-level feedback on design-oriented programming assignments. Designed to address the limitations of traditional autograding and overcome scaling challenges of formative assessment, FEEDBOT uses an existing pedagogical framework to provide targeted but limited actionable feedback. Early results demonstrate measurable improvements in student performance in a large introductory computer science course, while avoiding the pitfall of providing too much assistance that more unstructured tools commonly encounter. Although this experience report focuses on a particular implementation, we believe that FEEDBOT (and its general approach) is adaptable to many other contexts.

papers.title: Refinement or Disruption: Patterns of Critical Inquiry in
papers.authors: Michigan Technological University Houghton MI, Extreme Programming, On one hand, On the other hand
papers.abstract: Ethical inquiry in computing has an evolving nature, where repeated critical questioning may lead to a series of reframings of the problem. Since many computing students have experience with agile project-based courses, an iterative approach can provide a familiar entry into ethics. Agile development, however, is typically oriented around satisfaction of customer goals, while ethical inquiry requires constant questioning that may cast those goals into doubt. Does the similarity between critical ethical inquiry and iterative development provide a helpful model or breed a false familiarity? To address this question, we examine student work in a computing ethics course, involving iterative exercises using the Ethical Cycle. Through a qualitative analysis of students’ final projects, we examine the degree to which they take disruptive moves in their iterative inquiry, as opposed to steps of incremental refinement. We find that while most students are willing to make disruptive reformulations, the overall critical arcs of many students, including most of the high scoring students in our sample, have a refinement shape. We also find a pattern of expansive refinement that leads to a broad perspective on the moral problem with few disruptive moments. We also find critical arcs that do involve significant reformulations, but that this can indicate either a willingness to explore or a failure to engage fully in the moral problem.

papers.title: Deconstructing Engineering Students’ Ethical Reasoning: A
papers.authors: Consequentialist Framework for Algorithmic Choices Edward Kempa Ashish Aggarwal kempaedward@ufl.edu Department of Comp. and Info. Science and Engineering University of Florida Gainesville, Florida, US
papers.abstract: ACM Reference Format: Edward Kempa and Ashish Aggarwal. 2025. Deconstructing Engineering Students’ Ethical Reasoning: A Consequentialist Framework for Algorithmic Choices. In Proceedings of the 30th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education V. 1 (ITiCSE 2025), June 27July 2, 2025, Nijmegen, Netherlands. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 7 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3724363.3729048 The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) necessitates a comprehensive understanding of public receptivity to its applications. While computer science (CS) ethics education has focused on curriculum and teaching strategies, we’ve overlooked a crucial element: understanding students’ existing ethical perspectives. This gap limits our ability to assess the effectiveness of our teaching. How can we know if our ethics curriculum is relevant without first understanding our students’ viewpoints? This study aims to address this gap by investigating human decision-making (HDM) and perspectives on algorithmic decision-making in relation to varied payoffs and outcomes. We conducted two surveys among engineering students enrolled in an introductory programming course over two consecutive semesters in 2022, yielding 284 responses. The survey instrument assessed participants’ understanding of AI and their perspectives on its application in an ethically challenging autonomous vehicle scenario. Our analysis focused on responses to two questions with experimental variations, including differing consequences between the surveys. We employed an inductive qualitative analysis approach to identify significant themes in individual responses. Results indicate that engineering students’ perspectives on ethically complex scenarios were significantly influenced by controlled variance in consequences. Based on these findings, we developed a framework for tracing decision-making processes, linking participants’ choices to their underlying reasoning. This study provides insights into engineering students’ perceptions of AI applications, particularly in ethically nuanced contexts. These insights will contribute to developing better-informed discussions about ethics in computing courses.

papers.abstract: Functions are both an important and a difficult fundamental concept in introductory programming. This is also true for one particular part of functions, namely the keyword ‘return’. This work extended the research on this keyword, including the perspective of terms and explicit focus on misconceptions. We therefore investigated which terms novices typically use when describing code snippets of functions and which difficulties and misconceptions occur in these. We qualitatively analyzed more than 3,000 free-text responses from 617 undergraduate CS1 students using content analysis and thematic analysis. The keyword ‘return’ itself was rarely mentioned explicitly, unless a ‘void’ function made use of it. The aspect that the keyword ‘return’ ends the function was even less often explicitly mentioned. As a new misconception, some students stated that ‘return’ and ‘void’ are mutually exclusive. This study revealed overlap with established research as well as one new misconception and two variations of documented misconceptions.

papers.authors: Georgia State University Atlanta, Georgia State University Atlanta, Lipscomb University Nashville, USA Jonathan Calver Dastyni Loksa James Prather, University of Toronto Toronto, Towson University Towson, Abilene Christian University Abilene
papers.abstract: Keywords Introductory programming courses present a unique challenge for many students as a novel discipline, requiring significant time investment and featuring a steep learning curve, resulting in students experiencing high levels of failure while learning. Students’ perspectives on failure are crucial in determining how they confront these challenges and, consequently, their learning outcomes. This study investigates the relationship between undergraduate students’ views on failure–measured by validated scales about growth mindset, fear of failure, self-efficacy, and academic resilience–with their performance in introductory programming courses. While self-efficacy and growth mindset are well-studied in computing education, fear of failure and academic resilience remain understudied despite their prominence in other disciplines. We collected data from three universities to conduct a repeated measures study of 58 students’ attitudes toward failure at the beginning and the end of the semester. Our results indicated self-efficacy and fear of failure uniquely predicted performance, with lower self-efficacy and higher fear of failure related to poorer outcomes. Furthermore, students with lower self-efficacy and higher fear of failure were four times more likely to withdraw from or fail the course. Our findings suggest that measuring self-efficacy and fear of failure at the beginning of the semester can help identify at-risk students who need support. Research and interventions related to academic fear of failure from other STEM fields should be examined in the context of computing education to improve outcomes for our students. academic failure, computer science education, programming education, growth mindset, fear of failure, self-efficacy, academic resilience.

papers.abstract: CCS Concepts This study focuses on what classroom factors contribute to a positive educational experience and sense of material mastery for computing students. The CALI inventory, a tool to measure dimensions of Sociality, Structure, and Inclusivity features within computing courses, was combined with other metrics to evaluate how these environmental factors relate to students’ learning mindsets and perceived subject mastery. Data was collected from 381 computer science students about 580 course experiences at two universities in different regions of the country to address the following research questions: How do dimensions of course Sociality, Structure, and Inclusivity impact student perceived subject mastery? How do classroom dimensions and mastery relate to student learning mindsets? Our results indicate that sociality, structure and inclusivity are all positively and significantly associated with students’ perceived mastery. Students’ sense of belonging was also found to positively correlate with perceived mastery, though there were no significant associations between perceived mastery and other student mindset constructs of growth mindset, self-efficacy, grit and professional identity. Our approach contributes to computer science education research methodology and to a better understanding of pedagogical practices that can create more supportive and equitable education environments. • Social and professional topics → Computer science education.

papers.authors: Universidad de los Andes Santiago, University of Adelaide Adelaide, South Australia, University of Helsinki Helsinki, Finland Lisa Zhang, Carnegie Mellon University Pittsburgh, United States, University of Toronto Mississauga Mississauga
papers.abstract: Mastery learning was first defined in the late 1960s, but despite the promise of a student-focused methodology to establish firm foundations for later studies, it has not been widely adopted. In this paper, we consider why. We consider the evidence for mastery learning, and explore the organisational, structural, staffing, and pedagogical needs and challenges. We find, immediately, that there are competing implementations for mastery learning in computing education. We propose a way of representing pedagogical theories that use aspects of mastery learning in a way that allows a clear separation of techniques that appear similar but are not identical, to ensure the most appropriate implementation for a given area of application. These techniques still share similar challenges for adoption. We build towards possible solutions by considering recent developments in generative AI—and how these technologies could potentially provide automated assistants as a supporting component of mastery learning, in order to fully realise Bloom’s vision.

In particular, we will carry out a systematic literature review to address a wide set of issues and topics covering the rapidly emerging technology of GenAI from the perspective of its ethical and social impacts, we will provide an evaluation of university policies on the adoption and guidelines for use of GenAI for computing education and develop a framework to outline the ethical and societal impacts of GenAI in computing education. papers.title: Preparing Professionally Competent Computing Graduates:
papers.authors: The Role of Work Experiences Mihaela Sabin, New Hampshire, University of Glasgow Glasgow, Rochester Institute of Technology Rochester, New York, As Denning points out, At the same time, Work experiences must be a minor component, Work experiences must be a major component
papers.abstract: The academic preparation of computing graduates ready for successful long-term careers remains challenging due to a variety of factors, with most universities still unable to incorporate competencies into their education. Competencies refer to the knowledge, skills, and professional dispositions expected from these graduates during task performance. This panel presents three different perspectives on how work experiences may be incorporated into the program curriculum to develop the needed competencies.

papers.title: Bridge Programs: Pathways to Computing for All
papers.authors: Anu G. Bourgeois Georgia State University Atlanta, Wendy Fisher Colorado School of Mines Golden, DePaul University Chicago
papers.abstract: 1 The growing demand for computing professionals calls for innovative pathways that welcome individuals from non-computing backgrounds. Post-baccalaureate bridge programs help broaden access by supporting learners from diverse academic disciplines, career trajectories, and socioeconomic backgrounds. The MS Pathways to Computing (MSPC) Consortium, a network of 36 U.S. institutions, advances these efforts to create equitable pathways to master’s degrees in computer science. While U.S. bridge programs have gained momentum, they could have global impact. In many countries, early specialization and entrance exams limit flexibility for those who discover computing later. Bridge programs offer a structured, time- and cost-effective pathway for career changers, and adapting these models to fit different educational systems could create alternative entry points into computing. This session will engage an international audience in discussions on how bridge programs can be tailored to diverse contexts to broaden participation in computing and meet the global demand for skilled professionals. This panel will explore different models of computing bridge programs [1, 2], with a central focus on fostering inclusive learning environments that support individuals from non-STEM backgrounds, career changers, and groups historically underrepresented in computing. Panelists will examine the role of mentorship, academic advising, financial support, and employer engagement in helping students transition successfully into computing careers. Intended for educators, administrators, policymakers, and industry representatives, this panel will provide actionable insights on designing, implementing, and sustaining bridge programs. By sharing experiences and lessons learned, panelists will offer practical guidance for institutions looking to develop or enhance pathways into computing for non-traditional students. 2 SUMMARY PANEL FORMAT The panel will consist of a moderator and four panelists, featuring insights from institutions with established bridge programs, those in early implementation, and those preparing to launch. They represent a variety of institutions, including public, private, minorityserving, urban, rural, with fully in-person, and hybrid learning models. Each panelist brings a unique approach to the development and implementation of their programs, reflecting the diverse needs of their respective student populations. The session format will begin with each panelist sharing an overview of their bridge programs. The moderator will then facilitate a discussion with the panelists about the resources needed, challenges faced, and the types of students participating in their programs. Additionally, panelists will share insights on the benefits of belonging to the MSPC Consortium and the advantages of expanding to include global partners. The session will conclude with a Q&A segment, allowing both in-person and virtual participants to engage with the panelists.

papers.title: When People Come First: A Human-Centered Approach to Computer Science Education
papers.authors: JetBrains Research Belgrade, JetBrains Research Belgrade, Delft University of Technology Delft
papers.abstract: The rise of AI tools is reshaping computer science education, shifting the focus from coding skills to teaching students how to effectively use these technologies. Understanding students’ mental models and fostering computational and metacognitive skills are now essential, as over-reliance on AI can weaken critical thinking. This panel explores how a human-centered approach can balance these challenges, sharing strategies to optimize learning while addressing the risks of cognitive offloading in an AI-driven world.

papers.title: ShapeCreator Mobile: Practicing Coding at Home in Low-Resource Environments
papers.authors: McMaster University Hamilton, McMaster University Hamilton, McMaster University Hamilton, McMaster University Hamilton
papers.abstract: Access to STEM education is limited in many low-resource areas due to inadequate access to computers, the internet, trained educators, and reliable electricity. However, according to the GSM Association, over 54% of the global population owns a smartphone, presenting an opportunity for mobile-based learning solutions. To address this gap, we developed ShapeCreator Mobile, a learning tool designed to deliver our Algebraic Thinking curriculum to children with limited access to laptops but who own smartphones. This curriculum strengthens foundational math skills through coding, preparing students for high school algebra, a gateway to STEM careers. This approach bridges the digital divide and promotes inclusivity in STEM education in low-resource environments. Figure 1: Workflow including WebIDE (https://stabl.rocks), ShapeCreator, and ShapeCreator Mobile. communities, we designed ShapeCreator Mobile to bridge the accessibility gap in STEM education. This tool is the mobile version of the existing educational tool, ShapeCreator [3]. To use ShapeCreator [3] in the classroom, at least one computer with internet connection is needed. ShapeCreator Mobile allows the off-line coding of static graphics on their family smartphone to be assigned as homework to reinforce lessons. Figure 1 shows how homework assignments can feed into larger class and team projects integrated on a laptop through our WebIDE, maximizing the use of available technology. This approach combines ideas proven in two existing research projects. Bootstrap [6] has demonstrated that coding instructions based on a functional programming language can be designed to boost success in algebra. Additionally, Pocket Code [5] from the Catrobat project has demonstrated a block-based programming approach on smartphones.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a teaching material designed as part of a research project aiming to investigate approaches to teaching lower secondary school students technology-critical aspects of AI, specifically machine learning. The approach is scenario-based, meaning that students act in real-life roles, in this case in a fictional company that develops apps. The material has been tested in four classes in 2024, and analysis of the results is still ongoing. As part of our research, we examine whether and how a scenariobased approach contributes to understanding machine learning and its’ use in the real world. Preliminary analysis suggests that participating students perceive the approach differently. Methodologically, the material is developed and tested in an iterative design process in a collaboration between researchers and in-service teachers, and in an interdisciplinary context between biology and computer science, i.e. in the field of STEM. The teaching approach is scenario-based. This essentially means that the material is situated in a real-life scenario with the aim that students will be better able to apply their understanding of machine learning to the real world and not just understand it out of context (Fougt et al. 2022; Hanghøj et al., 2017). In the following, we present experts from the current version of the teaching material.

papers.abstract: Source code similarity detection tools are crucial for preventing and identifying plagiarism in programming courses. While tools like JPlag and Moss are effective, their complexity often hinders widespread adoption. To address this, we developed Dolos, a userfriendly source code similarity detection pipeline that enhances the user experience with interactive dashboards. The Dolos ecosystem includes software libraries, a CLI tool, a web UI, a web server, and API server enabling seamless integration with educational environments. The Dolos web server allows instructors to perform plagiarism detection directly within their browsers, eliminating the need for additional software installation. A publicly available instance and the option for private instances further enhance accessibility. Dolos’ API facilitates integration as a microservice within programming exercise platforms like Dodona, A+ and Radar, and Codio, showcasing its versatility and effectiveness. At Ghent University, Dolos is integral to the plagiarism detection strategy, with visualisations serving as both a detection tool and a deterrent. The focus on user experience, flexibility, and comprehensive documentation has attracted scholars to use Dolos for innovative applications, even outside of the educational field. We invite instructors to explore Dolos and integrate it within their educational platforms for programming assignments. Figure 1: Screenshot of the overview page shown by the Dolos UI. This interactive dashboard summarises the plagiarism detection results through its analytics and visualisations, providing an initial indication of whether plagiarism is prevalent within the analysed submissions. Additional visualisations of the most suspicious submissions and clusters lead to in-depth dashboards offering detailed views enabling further inspection. papers.abstract: Type-directed programming, where one uses the overall data structure and type signatures to drive programming, is a well known technique in functional programming. In a strongly typed language such as Haskell, type signatures provide valuable information and context to the function we are working with. Often the type signature alone is enough to define the body of a function or at least to understand the overall shape of the problem. Combining type-directed programming with a live programming lecturing style provides students with more tools to interrogate and define functions in a setting which is generally found difficult. The live programming setting is especially useful for providing guidance and insight on how to solve problems. Type-directed programming helps to provide shape and restriction to what students can implement, moving some weight from the lecturer’s explanations and onto the types.

papers.title: MeetingMayhem: A Web-Based Educational Game Focused on Adversarial Thinking
papers.authors: Shan Huang Geoffrey L. Herman, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign Urbana, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign Urbana, USA Linda Oliva Marc Olano, University of Maryland, Baltimore County Baltimore, USA Alan T. Sherman, University of Maryland, Baltimore County Baltimore, University of Maryland, Baltimore County Baltimore
papers.abstract: 1 MeetingMayhem is a web-based educational game focused on adversarial thinking in the context of network security. In particular, this game gently and non-technically introduces students without prior cybersecurity knowledge to the Dolev-Yao network intruder model. In MeetingMayhem, three students take on the roles of two agents and an adversary. Two agents need to agree on a time and location to exchange an essential asset. The agents communicate through a network controlled by the adversary without knowing the adversary’s identity. The adversary can insert, block, or modify messages. Students can play different roles, try different strategies, interact with different players, and send different messages. MeetingMayhem is available as a Docker Image, with open-source code. MeetingMayhem provides an engaging and innovative way for novice students to learn about adversarial thinking and cryptography within 2 hours. Adversarial thinking involves thinking and reasoning about adversaries’ actions and goals in a given context [7]. Many consider adversarial thinking to be the core concept of cybersecurity [4, 7– 9], and it is useful for everyone. For example, people who lack adversarial thinking may not realize that joining an unencrypted “free” public wifi network risks revealing their personal information. Despite widespread agreement on the importance of teaching adversarial thinking, the existing academic curriculum guidelines neglect this aspect of cybersecurity education [3]. Curricula that include adversarial thinking mainly focus on students in STEM majors [4]. Although adversarial thinking is important for everyone, we lack opportunities for students with limited technical backgrounds to learn it. To address this omission, we developed MeetingMayhem [5], a web-based educational game for college students focused on adversarial thinking in the context of network security. In MeetingMayhem, three students take on the roles of two agents and an adversary. MeetingMayhem is designed based on the Dolev-Yao (DY) model [2], which others have also used to teach adversarial thinking [1, 6] in courses. This paper highlights our MeetingMayhem tool; for user experiences, see [5]. The goal of the agents is to agree on a time and location to exchange an asset. The adversary is successful if they prevent the agreement. The agents do not need to hide the meeting time and location from the adversary. The agents communicate through a network controlled by the adversary without knowing the adversary’s identity. Although Alice knows that two agents and an adversary are present in the network, she is unaware of the identity of the adversary, who may be either Bob or Evan.

papers.title: AutoMCQ - Automatically Generate Code Comprehension Questions using GenAI
papers.authors: University of Strathclyde Glasgow, University of Strathclyde Glasgow, University of Strathclyde Glasgow, University of Strathclyde Glasgow
papers.abstract: 1 Students often do not fully understand the code they have written. This sometimes does not become evident until later in their education, which can mean it is harder to fix their incorrect knowledge or misunderstandings. In addition, being able to fully understand code is increasingly important in a world where students have access to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools, such as GitHub Copilot. One effective solution is to utilise code comprehension questions, where a marker asks questions about a submission to gauge understanding, this can also have the side effect of helping to detect plagiarism. However, this approach is time consuming and can be difficult and/or expensive to scale. This paper introduces AutoMCQ, which uses GenAI for the automatic generation of multiple-choice code comprehension questions. This is integrated with the CodeRunner automated assessment platform. Students in introductory programming classes are generally able to write working code. However, they may not have a full understanding or comprehension of how the code works. In the experience of Lehtinen et al., around a third of their class of 125 students had difficulties explaining their code [2]. At this introductory stage, this can have serious long term consequences to the student’s ability to become a skilled programmer, as these shaky foundations become increasingly strained by problems of greater scale and complexity. Code comprehension questions are an effective solution to this problem [4], forcing students to critically examine their own code, as well as challenging any incorrect assumptions. Unfortunately, the bespoke nature - manually creating questions based on a student’s own code, makes for a process which is difficult to scale to larger classes. This work presents AutoMCQ, a tool for the automatic generation of bespoke multiple-choice code comprehension questions by utilising a combination of automated unit testing and AI generated follow-up questions. This is not necessarily intended as a method of assigning or gating class credit, but rather as a tool for identifying cases where there might be a benefit to early intervention.

papers.title: CyberGuardian: A Role-Playing Educational Game for Learning Cryptographic Primitives in Authentic Cybersecurity Scenarios
papers.authors: Shan Huang, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign Urbana, USA Geoffrey L. Herman, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign Urbana, This awareness promotes better practices
papers.abstract: CyberGuardian is an interactive educational game that introduces students to foundational concepts in cybersecurity through authentic scenarios. Specifically, the game teaches students about cryptographic primitives and adversarial thinking. Targeted at students without computer science backgrounds, the game immerses players in practical cybersecurity challenges using simplified technical concepts. Players assume the role of a cybersecurity advisor, providing guidance to simulated clients and analyzing authentic messages to assure confidentiality, data integrity, and authentication through three cryptographic primitives: symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption, and digital signature. Implemented as a single-player offline experience on Mac and Windows, CyberGuardian is scalable and broadly available.

papers.title: Communicating StateCharts (CSC)
papers.authors: Sheida Emdadi, McMaster University Hamilton, Canada Spencer Smith, McMaster University Hamilton, Canada Christopher Kumar Anand, McMaster University Hamilton
papers.abstract: 2 We propose a new concurrency framework called Communicating StateCharts (CSC) with the potential to simplify the teaching concurrency to beginners. CSC was designed based on five main principles chosen to reduce barriers for beginners: using software visualization, Model-Driven Development (MDD), pure functions, Separation of Concerns (SoC), and—most importantly—raising the level of abstraction. To address these principles, we adopted features from existing concurrency models (i.e., process calculi and the actor model) in alignment with the principles, resulting in CSC’s atomic statecharts, communicating through channels. We also present CSCDraw, a visual MDD tool to support CSC. CSC tries to achieve its goal of supporting beginners by considering five main principles: (P1) Raise abstraction to handle complexities by using Event-Driven Programming (EDP). Specifically, EDP increases abstraction through using events instead of threads, and allows programmers to make interactive applications such as games, which is a frequent strategy used to motivate beginners [7]. To further increase the engagement of EDP, and exploit its success in making concurrency easier, we put the focus of CSC on allowing the design of multi-player games. (P2) Visualizing the system through statecharts, the most commonly used modelling language in the case of interactive applications [12]. We believe that visualization will contribute to simplification by reducing the cognitive load, analogous to how it has helped students correct misconceptions about object-oriented programming [14]. (P3) Using Model-Driven Development (MDD) to generate code from visual models. This code generation relieves beginners from repetitive coding and can protect them from many flaws caused by typos and incomplete understanding, preventing early frustration. (P4) Using pure functions and generating purely functional, skeleton code based on the designed models. Distributed concurrency can be expressed using pure functions in the recently introduced architecture, Local-Global Model-View-Update (LG-MVU) [13]. LG-MVU separates the program into local (private to each user) and global (shared among every client connected to the server) portions, all without losing the transparency afforded by pure functions. (P5) Separation of Concerns (SoC) through isolation of models. In particular, message passing via channels should replace direct transitions between statecharts.

Therefore, developing high-quality teaching materials remains a significant challenge. This study proposes a STEAM interdisciplinary-integrated instructional model focusing on programming learning, uses this model to develop teaching materials and design instructional activities, and evaluates student learning outcomes. STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts & Mathematics) integrated instructional approach not only increases students' interest in learning hard science but also enhances their understanding in arts. We proposed a five-step STEAM interdisciplinary-integrated instructional model to teach student programming, which are: choosing an art example, inspiring creativity, hands-on design, programming implementation, optimizing and sharing. We used the model to design materials to teach middle school student modular programming with the Mandala Art design. The results showed that the proposed STEAM model promoted students' learning, enhanced their understanding of art concepts, and inspired students' thinking. 2 STEAM INTERDISCIPLINARYINTEGRATED INSTRUCTIONAL MODEL We invited professors from computer sciences and art education, along with middle school computing teachers and art teachers, to collaboratively develop the STEAM interdisciplinary instructional model centered on programming learning. First of all, in order to integrate art into the programming course, teacher needs to find out the relevant topics of programming from the art course that fits the students' grade level. In class, teacher guides students to understand the meaning of the work and the design process. Then, programming concepts are introduced and combined with the artistic elements. Finally, students practice and create their own works using programming to share with their peers. The model consists of five steps: choosing an art example related to programming, inspiring creativity, hands-on design, programming implementation, optimizing and sharing.

papers.authors: Ethan Fong University of Toronto Toronto, Michelle Craig University of Toronto Toronto, To understand what makes an interesting feature
papers.abstract: Educational puzzles can be a powerful way to develop the situational interest of learners by presenting an authentic and challenging experience. This is important because situational interest has been shown to be a key predictor of engagement and performance. To this end, we developed CS Connections, inspired by the New York Times Connections puzzle game. CS Connections is a tool that provides educators with a flexible way to create custom interactive puzzles in a familiar format. This paper presents tips and techniques on how to create puzzles that make the most of CS Connections’ features, and how we designed these features with learners’ interest in mind. We also provide example puzzles and design insights from a CS1 course where the tool has been used. CS Connections is open source and available online, giving educators the flexibility to sample and seamlessly integrate the tool into their teaching. • Authenticity The degree to which activities reflect realworld applications and computing practices. • Challenge The appropriate level of difficulty that engages learners, ideally adjustable to an individual’s needs. • Usefulness The extent to which learners perceive the activity as contributing to their broader learning goals. • Meaningfulness How much activities align with students’ personal values, enabling them to pursue work that resonates with their identities.

papers.abstract: We present a didactical tool in the form of an interactive Large Language Model (LLM) application that allows users to develop a better understanding of prompt construction. To achieve this, the application includes a modular, interactive prompt construction tool that allows end-users to generate prompt variations and explore how different prompt characteristics influence the reliability of the output. The tool takes a prompt, optimizes it based on selected parameters, and provides the LLM response to the optimized prompt. The visualization of the differences between the prompt variations and the differences between the corresponding model results, allows users to develop a better understanding of how specific prompt characteristics can affect the reliability of LLM outputs.

papers.title: Getting Used to Pointers with Pointer Drills
papers.authors: Michael Guerzhoy Division of Engineering Science University of Toronto Toronto, Ontario, Canada
papers.abstract: 2 When you start out reading C code, reading code can feel like reading a foreign language: you get lost in a sea of asterisks, dots, arrows, and ampersands. Experienced C programmers write pointer code the way fluent users of math and language write: they do not necessarily always need to reason from first principles. We propose learning to use pointers the way students learn algebra in school: doing a large number of small exercises. John von Neumann famously said that "[i]n mathematics, you don’t understand things. You just get used to them." We hope that our drill exercises enable both getting used to pointers and understanding them. Our exercises and solutions are available at https://CPointerDrills.github.io/. We aimed to produce a large number of short exercises that would be comprehensive in introducing students to different ways of using pointers in C, in the context of operating on an object, a block (an array or a malloc-allocated block) of objects, or a block of pointers to objects1 . Since the aim is to teach pointer arithmetic, we aim to keep the context familiar to all students: we use students’ names, student numbers, and grades.

papers.title: Aggregate-Superpose-Project: A Cognitive Model for Quantum Problem Solving
papers.authors: Michigan Technological University Houghton MI
papers.abstract: This work proposes a novel cognitive model, called AggregateSuperpose-Project (ASP), to facilitate problem solving and the analysis of algorithms in Quantum Computing (QC). Our model contains three simple abstractions that help students use classic computing concepts towards specifying quantum states and transformations. Simplicity is a major advantage of ASP along with reinforcing the use of classical concepts in learning QC abstractions. Preliminary evaluations indicate that ASP can provide students with the means to describe quantum algorithms at appropriate levels of abstraction. Figure 1: The ASP model.

papers.title: A Comparison of On-Demand Hints and Progress Bar Feedback on Programming Exercises
papers.authors: University of Toronto Toronto, University of Toronto Toronto, North Carolina State University Raleigh, North Carolina, University of Toronto Toronto
papers.abstract: We conducted this study in a 12-week CS1 course with 1,260 students, following the University of Toronto ethics protocol #31881. Students solving Python exercises [3] were randomly assigned, with equal probability, to either receive hints or not. An end-of-term survey (1% bonus) included Likert-scale and open-ended questions on student perceptions of the hints. Of the respondents, 68 experienced both hint systems, 227 only on-demand hints, and 94 only progress bar feedback. Responses were categorized into paired (experienced both types of hints) and independent subsets for analysis. This pilot study investigated students’ perceptions of visual progress bar and on-demand hints in a CS1 course. Students valued both feedback systems, with more confident students preferring on-demand hints for direct problem-solving support. Progress bars were consistently perceived as beneficial across varying confidence levels.

papers.title: Self-Explanations: Does Timing Matter?
papers.authors: ESPOL Guayaquil, ESPOL Guayaquil, McMaster University Hamilton, ESPOL Guayaquil, University of Toronto Mississauga
papers.abstract: 2 Self-explanation promotes active learning by having students articulate their conceptual understanding in their own words. This study investigates whether the timing of self-explanations (before vs. after solving an exercise) relates to performance in a flipped, second-year computer organization course. Although students who self-explained before the exercises achieved higher course marks, the difference was not significant. Still, these findings suggest that early self-explanation may better prepare students for problemsolving when learning new concepts. Our data includes 71 students who completed self-explanations before the exercise and 47 who did so afterward. It suggests a potential benefit of early self-explanation, as the mean grade of the “before” group was higher (78.31 vs. 72.69). A MANOVA followed by a post-hoc t-test (𝑡 (82.5) = 1.83, 𝑝 = 0.07; Cohen’s 𝑑 = 0.36) reveals that this difference is not statistically significant, but 60% of students reported using the self-explanation activity to plan their approach, indicating that students perceive the exercise to be valuable preparation. Our study indicates that students who complete self-explanations before tackling exercises may perform better, potentially because early reflection aids in planning and clarifying understanding. However, since students self-selected their timing, it is possible that higher-performing students naturally opted for pre-exercise selfexplanation. Future research should employ random assignment to pre- and post-explanation conditions and extend the study across different courses. Including more detailed qualitative data and examining long-term retention could further clarify the role of timing in self-explanation effectiveness.

papers.title: Enhancing Self-Explanation in Student Learning
papers.authors: McMaster University Hamilton, University of Toronto Mississauga, University of Toronto Mississauga
papers.abstract: 2 Self-explanation deepens understanding by giving learners an opportunity to reflect on what they are learning in a structured way. However, many students struggle to engage in it effectively. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can scaffold selfexplanations in a flipped computer organization course. In an A/B test, one group used a fixed prompt to compare their explanations with an expert’s, while another engaged in an interactive dialogue with an LLM to identify gaps. Although the overall quality of the explanation did not differ significantly between conditions, some students (non-native English speakers and women) reported greater comfort and perceived value when using the LLM. Two researchers reviewed a subset of 20 self-explanations from both the control and treatment groups, agreeing on a codebook to evaluate the rest. The researchers used this codebook to review 49 explanations from the control group and 43 explanations from the treatment group. We did not see statistically significant differences in overall explanation quality (𝑝 > 0.05), and end-of-term survey results indicated that the overall student experience was similar across groups. However, subgroup analysis revealed that non-native English speakers in the LLM condition reported approximately a 15% higher rating in comfort and perceived learning compared to the control condition. Similarly, women in the treatment group rated the self-explanation process 10–15% more favorably across dimensions of learning, comfort, value, and convenience. Inductive coding of student responses indicated that while many students did not revise their explanations after receiving feedback, those who engaged with the LLM noted its ability to highlight overlooked aspects of the material. However, several students remarked that the LLM’s responses felt generic, perhaps due to limitations posed on the timing and number of interactions provided. Our study did not reveal significant improvements in explanation quality when using an LLM, the enhanced user experience reported by non-native English speakers and women is promising. The 10–15% boost in perceived value among targeted subgroups suggests that a more integrated and personalized LLM interaction may yield stronger benefits. Future work should focus on increasing the frequency and timing of LLM interventions and incorporating richer qualitative methods (e.g., think-aloud protocols) to better understand and harness their potential in educational settings.

papers.title: Enhancing Cybersecurity Mindset through Rock-Paper-Scissors: A Hands-On Approach to Adversarial Thinking
papers.authors: El Paso Community College El Paso, Data Structures. In this poster, CIA Triad, Conference attendees
papers.abstract: Adversarial Thinking (AT) is a fundamental component of cybersecurity and computing education, promoting strategic thinking and problem-solving by anticipating worst-case scenarios. The integration of AT into early computing courses, particularly in the first two years of college, remains underexplored. This challenge is especially pronounced in the US Community Colleges, where students prepare for both workforce entry and transfer opportunities. This poster presents an innovative approach to embedding AT into fundamental computer science courses using the traditional game rock-paper-scissors as an educational model. Through this analogy, key cybersecurity concepts are introduced, along with adversarial interactions such as brute force attacks, phishing, encryption, and social engineering. By fostering AT at the foundational level, students can develop stronger problem-solving skills, cybersecurity awareness, and preparedness for advanced computing courses and careers.

papers.title: Gen AI in Computing Education: A Gap Analysis of Pedagogical Practices and Industry Expectations
papers.authors: Arnel B. Ocay† Maria Mercedes T. Rodrigo Ateneo de Manila University Quezon City, Philippines arnelocay@ucu.edu.ph Department of Information Systems and Computer Science Ateneo de Manila University Qu
papers.abstract: questions were asked to industry practitioners, and the data were analyzed using themes. Traditional software development relied heavily on manual coding handled solely by human programmers, assisted by smart editors and IDEs. With the rise of Gen AI, much of the coding and debugging process has been automated, significantly improving productivity. For instance, Amazon reported saving 4,500 manyears and $260 million using its AI tool in 2024. This shift raises questions for computing education: What skills should students learn if coding can be automated? To answer the question for this paper, we analyzed mixed data from industry practitioners regarding the essential skills computing students need to acquire. Findings show that industry underscores foundational programming skills such as strong programming logic, algorithms, and knowledge in data structure (Mean= 3.79), and analytical and problem-solving skills (Mean= 3.95). Notably, AIrelated skills were highly emphasized, particularly the ability to ask precise and contextually relevant prompts for Gen AI tools (Mean=3.84), the capability to assess the correctness and applicability of AI-generated code (Mean=4.16), and the capability to evaluate AI-generated code for quality measures (Mean=3.74, SD=3.40). These results suggest that while the industry adopts an AI-assisted coding workflow, developing foundational programming and AI-enhanced coding skills must be prioritized to prepare students for the demands of the industry. The study explores the gaps between current teaching practices and industry expectations, involving (n=26) teachers and (n=19) industry practitioners in the Philippines through a mixed-methods survey. Findings highlight the need for students to develop both foundational computing skills and AI-related competencies, such as prompt engineering and integrating AI tools into development workflows.

papers.title: Exploring Making in Early Childhood Education: Initial Insights from an Intervention with Preschool Students
papers.authors: University of Potsdam Potsdam, University of Stuttgart Stuttgart
papers.abstract: Making and digital fabrication have been increasingly incorporated into computing education to attract female students, foster creativity, and promote design thinking through the hands-on creation of tangible products. While makerspaces and Making activities have been widely integrated into primary and secondary education, their application in early childhood education (ECE) remains limited. This work presents initial findings from a study exploring the integration of Making in ECE. A total of 49 preschool students participated in the intervention, with their future skills assessed using the Positive Technological Behaviour (PTB) rubric. Results indicate medium to high mean values across PTB dimensions, with the highest scores observed in students’ choices of conduct and communication. Conversely, creativity and collaboration exhibited the lowest scores, prompting discussion on potential contributing factors. These findings offer valuable preliminary insights into the role of Making in ECE and lay the groundwork for further investigation in this emerging area. Figure 1: Mean values of the observed PTBs for the learning activities LA2, 5, and 6. Higher values indicate better results. programming and Making have been explored as effective methods for introducing computing concepts to young learners [2–4]. Initial research suggests that Making interventions can support the development of these essential skills [2–4], yet longitudinal analyses remain scarce. This study involved 49 preschool students (23 male, 26 female) across four kindergartens, participating in a nine-session Making intervention. The intervention included six hands-on learning activities (LA), such as constructing (LA1) and electrifying a house (LA2), creating an illuminated painting (LA3), building a city with electrical circuits (LA4), crafting a brush robot (LA5), and designing a moving companion (LA6) [1]. Each session, lasting between 30 and 90 minutes, emphasized collaborative work, enabling students to develop process-related skills, including communication, design thinking, fine motor skills, and tool usage. Student progress was assessed using the Positive Technological Behaviour (PTB) rubric [2–4]. As shown in Figure 1, PTB assessments were conducted at three points: the beginning, middle, and end of the intervention. Results indicated high scores in communication and choices of conduct, while creativity and collaboration exhibited lower to medium values, highlighting areas for further exploration.

We developed our taxonomy with the aim of creating a good basis for developing effective assessment tools and teaching interventions.

papers.title: Flipping the Final: Individualized Learning through a Teaching-Based Assessment
papers.authors: This poster explores an alternative, In this teaching-based final exam, Instead of answering standardized test questions, Prepare a mini-lecture, To assess their experiences, I collected subjective feedback on engagement, They also expressed a preference for this format, Future work will explore scalability
papers.abstract: Traditional final exams in introductory computer science courses often rely on one-size-fits-all testing, which may not support individual learning needs. Research on mastery learning suggests that students learn more effectively when focusing on weak areas and actively constructing knowledge. This poster presents a teachingbased final exam that promotes individualized learning. Students are assigned a challenging topic related to their weaknesses and tasked with preparing a mini-lecture, designing a quiz, and creating an exam-level problem with a rubric. This final exam shifts assessment from passive recall to active learning by requiring students to reconstruct knowledge and engage in peer instruction, reinforcing conceptual understanding. Subjective feedback on engagement, confidence, and perceived learning outcomes suggests that students found this approach more effective and engaging than traditional exams. This poster describes the design of this teaching-based assessment, shares student reflections, and discusses the implications and limitations of individualized learning in computer science education.
