papers.title: KOALA: Customizable IDE Data Collection Tool
papers.authors: JetBrains Research Munich, JetBrains Research Belgrade, Utrecht University Utrecht, JetBrains Research Belgrade
papers.abstract: 2 Collecting data from students solving programming tasks is valuable for both researchers and educators. Such data can be used to analyze student behavior, identify errors and misconceptions, and for many other purposes. In this work, we propose KOALA, a configurable tool to collect student data using JetBrains IDEs. This tool collects code snapshots and IDE interactions, converts them into the ProgSnap2 format, and provides visualization analysis. Tool workflow. The data collection process starts with setting up the tool using YAML files to define coding tasks, IDE settings, and data collection details, e.g., granularity of the collected data. The tool is then shared with students and installed in their IDEs, working across different programming languages with a single configuration format. It saves the data both locally and on a remote server. Privacy policy. KOALA protects student data by requiring consent before collection and only tracking code from specified files. Collected data. KOALA collects diverse data, including code snapshots, IDE activities (e.g., running code or debugging), file interactions, tool window usage, and survey responses. Additionally, it can integrate and collect data from third-party tools specified via configuration. The data can be converted into the ProgSnap2 [6] format for easy use with existing research tools. Data visualization. The tool includes a dashboard to facilitate the analysis of the collected data. It provides basic statistics, such as the total number of participants and general study information, along with detailed insights into frequently used IDE actions or IDE windows, as well as the focus time during the study. This tool enables researchers to better interpret the data and generate preliminary insights efficiently. Discussion. We already used KOALA to collect several datasets with students’ task solving process, showing the effectiveness of the tool. We hope that this poster will spark discussions about the future direction of this project and how we can make it even more useful to the community.

papers.title: Can GPT4 Generate Effective Feedback on Code Readability?
papers.authors: McGill University Montreal, College London London, McGill University Montreal, ETH Zurich Zurich, For a pilot study
papers.abstract: Effective feedback is often timely and consistent but, with large cohorts, this is not always achievable. This study explored the potential of GPT4 to generate feedback on code readability for students enrolled in a CS1 Java course. We developed rubrics based on three readability criteria: naming, commenting, and formatting. We defined feedback criteria and incorporated them into GPT4 prompts to guide feedback generation. Results were mixed: while some feedback messages closely aligned with the rubrics, offering valuable insights, others fell short in providing corrective guidance. This highlights the potential and limitations of using LLMs to generate feedback on code readability. Future research could refine these methods to improve feedback consistency and quality. Results & Discussion The evaluation of GPT4-generated feedback across five submissions suggested that 24 out of 25 feedback instances aligned with the five predefined guidelines, whereas one instance did not refer to student code. Naming conventions: all five feedback instances addressed meaningful variable names but one was incorrect. Code commenting: all feedback instances were accurate in their analysis but one overlooked the spelling errors in the student code. Formatting: only one instance correctly addressed indentation, blank lines, and white space use. The results showed that GPT4 was weak in addressing structural code quality. Results suggest that GPT4 shows promise in generating feedback aligned with predefined guidelines, especially on variable naming, concomitantly revealing areas for improvement, particularly in feedback accuracy. The variability in feedback accuracy points to refined guidelines, better prompts, and a more detailed definition of code readability. Future work will refine our definition of code readability, expand to a broader range of examples, and explore the performance of GPT4 across various programming tasks and readability criteria.

papers.title: Using Large Language Models to Develop Requirements
papers.authors: University of California, Berkeley Berkeley, University of Sevilla Sevilla, SCORE Lab, University of Sevilla Sevilla, SCORE Lab, University of Sevilla Sevilla, Spain Rohan Philip, Oak Park High School Oak Park, USA Armando Fox, University of California, Berkeley Berkeley, SCORE Lab, University of Sevilla Sevilla, Spain Team skills, One such skill is requirements elicitation, In formal higher education
papers.abstract: Requirements Elicitation (RE) is a crucial software engineering skill that involves interviewing a client and then devising a software design based on the interview results. We propose conditioning a large language model to play the role of the client during a chatbased interview. We evaluate our approach in a study (𝑛 = 120) using both a qualitative survey and quantitative observations about participants’ work. Our positive findings suggest a new way to practice critical RE skills in a scalable and realistic manner without the overhead of arranging live interviews.

papers.title: Integrating Version Control Systems into Computer Science Curricula: Challenges and Experiences Mari Raavel
papers.authors: VCS basics, All learning resources
papers.abstract: Version Control Systems (VCS) have become essential in the soware industry, enabling eﬀective team collaboration, change tracking, and code quality assurance. Despite these clear advantages, adopting tools like Git in educational contexts oen faces resistance from faculty and practical challenges when embedding them into teaching practices. Drawing from our experience in developing an applied computer science bachelor’s program, this study explores the ways of early and continuous VCS integration, examines why some educators remain hesitant to adopt these tools, and suggests feasible approaches to facilitate successful implementation.

papers.title: Sorting the Universe: Learning Success and Perception of Flow in an Immersive Game for Training Sorting Algorithms
papers.authors: Daniel Unro Andreas Dengel, Goethe University Frankfurt Frankfurt, Goethe University Frankfurt Frankfurt, Germany immersive educational game
papers.abstract: Sorting algorithms serve as a fundamental concept in computer science education, yet maintaining student motivation remains a challenge. This pilot study investigates whether virtual reality (VR) offers advantages over traditional desktop-based settings in terms of learning success and flow perception, using a self-designed educational game that teaches three sorting algorithms. Learning success and flow perception were assessed through pre- and posttests across both settings. Results indicate no significant differences between VR and desktop settings in either learning success or flow experience. 2 Integration of Virtual Reality Games in Computing Education Game-based learning integrates educational content into engaging digital experiences, potentially increasing motivation and cognitive retention [7]. Flow theory highlights that the flow state fosters deep concentration, intrinsic motivation, and an optimal learning experience by fully immersing individuals in the task at hand. [1, 7]. VR offers an immersive learning environment that may enhance engagement and facilitate flow [2, 3]. Prior research indicates that combining game-based learning and VR can create a state of flow, improve motivation and knowledge retention, but its impact on computational learning remains unclear [4, 5].

papers.title: AI in Computational Thinking Education in Higher Education: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.authors: Ebrahim Rahimi Clara Maathuis Open University, Computer Science department Heerlen, Open University, Computer Science department Heerlen
papers.abstract: 1 Computational Thinking (CT) is a key skill set for students in higher education to thrive and adapt to an increasingly technologydriven future and workplace. While research on CT education has gained remarkable momentum in K-12 over the past decade, it has remained under-explored in higher education, leaving higher education teachers with an insufficient overview, knowledge, and support regarding CT education. The proliferation and adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) by educational institutions have demonstrated promising potential to support instructional activities across many disciplines, including CT education. However, a comprehensive overview outlining the various aspects of integrating AI in CT education in higher education is lacking. To mitigate this gap, we conducted this systematic literature review study. The focus of our study is to identify initiatives applying AI in CT education within higher education and to explore various educational aspects of these initiatives, including the benefits and challenges of AI in CT education, instructional strategies employed, CT components covered, and AI techniques and models utilized. This study provides practical and scientific contributions to the CT education community, including an inventory of AI-based initiatives for CT education useful to educators, an overview of various aspects of integrating AI into CT education—such as its benefits and challenges (e.g., AI’s potential to reshape CT education versus its potential to diminish students’ creativity)—and insights into new and expanded perspectives on CT in light of AI (e.g., the ’decoding’ approach alongside the ’coding’ approach to CT). Computational Thinking (CT) is an important set of thinking skills that students need to thrive and adapt to the future, yet it remains a largely underexplored topic in higher education compared to K–12. AI has emerged as a disruptive technology in CT education (e.g., CT 2.0 [2]). We conducted this systematic literature review to identify the educational and technological aspects of integrating AI into CT education in higher education, including its benefits and challenges, underlying instructional strategies, covered CT concepts and practices, and the AI methods employed.

papers.title: ‘AI Training Should Be for Everyone’: Informal Training on AI
papers.authors: Maria Kasinidou Open University of Cyprus Nicosia, Guarda Guarda, CYENS Nicosia
papers.abstract: We all interact with AI daily, however, our understanding of it often remains limited. We present a training conducted as part of an Erasmus YE, with 36 individuals aged 18 to 30 from Austria, Armenia, Bulgaria, Latvia, Poland and Portugal. Our findings indicate that participants improved their AI literacy and recognized the value of such training, expressing that AI training is useful for everyone. 3

papers.title: AI Debugging Assistant: Enhancing Debugging
papers.authors: JetBrains Research Berlin, JetBrains Research Belgrade, JetBrains Research Belgrade
papers.abstract: Debugging is an essential skill in programming education. Current debugging approaches lack interactivity and personalization for students. To address this gap, we introduce an AI Debugging Assistant integrated into JetBrains IDEs. The tool analyzes the students’ errors in real-time and guides them through the debugging process by recommending breakpoints and explaining them on each step. This poster invites discussion on the effectiveness of the AI Debugging Assistant and its implications for programming education. 2

papers.title: Learning About Technical Debt via an Educational Board Game
papers.authors: Eva Krebs eva.krebs@hpi.uni-potsdam.de Hasso Plattner Institute University of Potsdam Potsdam, Germany Luc Maurice Prestin l.prestin@gmx.de Hasso Plattner Institute University of Potsdam Potsdam, Germ
papers.abstract: Software development is typically not taught and experienced primarily through books and lectures but instead through practice. However, university teaching entails time constraints, creating a mismatch between the theoretical knowledge from lectures and the practical challenges students face in accompanying projects. Trade-offs of selected practices might not apply, or not apply clearly enough, for students to experience and reflect on them. We want lectures to be able to demonstrate topics and challenges not yet covered by the accompanying project by using an interactive teaching method: board games. In our experimental game, students learn about the basics of iterative development processes and balancing related activities such as refactoring. In small teams, students collaboratively have to make decisions in a simplified software engineering process. This poster presents our game and preliminary work on evaluating our approach. 2 Poster Content In this poster, we will describe our educational board game, its intended learning goals, and our main design decisions. The game simulates an iterative software development process where students play co-operatively in small groups. Players must balance working on tickets (since otherwise they lose the game), refactoring the code base (as technical debt increases ticket cost), and events outside their influence (represented by event cards and effects of closed tickets). A pilot run of our game as an onboarding exercise in our mandatory undergraduate software engineering course was well received. We still face open challenges, such as a more in-depth evaluation of whether and how our game succeeds in teaching its intended learning goals.

papers.title: Multimodal Analogy Generation in Programming Education
papers.authors: JetBrains Research Belgrade, Delft University of Technology Delft
papers.abstract: Engaging students with effective learning materials continues to be a significant challenge in programming education. Analogies are commonly used to simplify complex topics, enabling learners to relate unfamiliar concepts to familiar ones. Additionally, visual representations of these analogies can enhance engagement and improve the overall learning experience. This work presents a prototype of a novel AI tool that generates analogy-based explanations and corresponding video animations for programming education. The tool leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) for analogy generation and a structured animation workflow for visualization. This poster invites discussion on the effectiveness of AI-generated educational content and its implications for programming education. (a)

papers.title: AI Exploratorium: A Gamified Approach to AI Literacy through
papers.authors: Experiential Learning in Interactive Exhibitions Tina Maljur† Jasminko Novak Jessica Laufer Sarah Gnoth European Institute for Participatory Media Berlin, Germany t.maljur@eipcm.org Institute for Appl
papers.abstract: exhibition. It is based on a structured AI literacy framework [2], which was refined in the iKIDO project [3]. The didactical implementation focuses on problem-based learning and selfdirected exploration with limited facilitator guidance. It includes four main stations, each presenting a challenge (an “AI puzzle”) related to a specific real AI use case. All participants start with training a machine learning model for image recognition for a simulated autonomous car. They experiment with choosing and labelling training data in teams and test their model in a simulated test drive, competing for best score. Other challenges add new insights: e.g. a deep fake detection card game shifts the modality from digital to analogue, and introduces the topic of AI image generation. The “catch me if you can” challenge addresses the use of AI in public surveillance systems, expanding on ethical issues in AI use. Through challenges students learn how AI systems for image recognition and generation work, and what is needed for responsible use. In the final challenge where they develop an AI application (no-code) for a problem they care about. Quick quizzes support reflection after each challenge. For each solved challenge, the hidden parts of the “black box” of AI, displayed on a projection screen, are revealed with the obtained learnings. First user tests show that the AI Exploratorium is an engaging learning experience, supporting AI literacy and critical reflection on AI use. At the poster session, we want to exchange ideas and discuss challenges and opportunities of integrating such approaches for AI education in schools, youth spaces and museums, building AI literacy in an engaging and critical way. This poster presents an experiential learning approach for supporting the acquisition of basic AI competences for highschool students. AI Exploratorium is an experimental, interactive and gamified learning space where students learn main principles of training and building machine learning AI systems and understand the importance of responsible AI use. It consists of several hands-on challenges (puzzles) within the format of an interactive exhibition. In solving the puzzles students train AI models, analyze and reflect on their outcomes and limitations. They explore several AI application areas (e.g. automation and surveillance), and discuss ethical aspects. This helps them develop a critical awareness and understand trade-offs between potential benefits and risks of AI. The exploratory nature supports students’ sense of autonomy, while gamified puzzles set in real use cases make AI concepts relevant to young learners.

papers.title: Large Language Models with Reasoning on Theory Course Exams
papers.authors: United States Military Academy West Point, New York, United States Military Academy West Point, New York, United States Military Academy West Point, New York
papers.abstract: Theory of Computing (ToC) courses are important in CS curricula as they promote formal reasoning and writing skills about computation. Large language models (LLMs) have recently upended standard pedagogy in CS courses, but ToC courses have so far been fairly resistant to LLMs as they generally have lacked reasoning abilities. Prior work showed that GPT-4 performed at an “average" student level, specifically with a B-/C+ average. Considerable advancements since that prior work have occurred with LLMs in that some now provide “reasoning" capabilities. In this poster we tested whether the ChatGPT o1 LLM can perform better than GPT-4 on our ToC course’s exams. We found that o1 can solve ToC questions approximately two letter grades higher than GPT-4 could, specifically at an A+ level. Midterm 1 Midterm 2 Final Exam Average GPT-4 Initial 80.5% 87.5% 81.0% 82.3% GPT-4 + Retry 93.0% 92.0% 88.6% 90.3% o1 99.0% 100.5% 103.2% 101.7% of 28 questions (79%). Note that there were many “near misses”, in that all but one question (96%) had a score of at least 70%. We have shown that LLMs can completely solve a large majority of traditional ToC questions. We recommend that ToC educators remove any graded homework or at least severely limit their weight. If that is an option, ask questions in a way that does not reveal the answer in the question, e.g., instead of asking “Prove 𝐿 is not regular”, instead ask: “Is 𝐿 regular? True or False, and prove your answer.” In a similar vein, keep graded work in-class without access to electronic devices as much as possible. Finally, require that students give detailed proofs in any unsupervised, graded work. There is much interesting research to do. What other pedagogical uses in ToC courses are there with a reasoning model like o1? How does o1 perform in graduate-level courses? Can o1 automatically grade ToC coursework? Answering these questions will be of great use to ToC educators.

papers.title: Find One Solution that Solves both Problems!
papers.authors: Karlsruhe University of Education Karlsruhe
papers.abstract: Introducing algorithmic problem-solving in K-12 beginner programming classes requires scaffolding methods that structure both the selection and sequencing of problems. In response to calls for a stronger emphasis on abstraction-oriented teaching, in this poster a new idea for introducing algorithmic problem-solving is proposed. Students are presented with two structurally equivalent problems, which they must compare and solve concurrently with a common algorithmic solution. Here, the approach and the design of a mixedmethods study investigating its effectiveness are presented. 2 Methods & Next Steps A quasi-experimental mixed-methods study was designed (Fig. 1). The current research question is: RQ1: How does simultaneous problem presentation with analogous problems foster algorithmic abstraction compared to sequential problem presentation? Once the data collected has been analyzed, initial results will be reported and simultaneous problem presentation will be tested in different settings.

papers.title: "Can You Refactor This for Me?": Investigating How Students Use ChatGPT in Code Refactoring Exercises
papers.authors: Eduardo Carneiro Oliveira Utrecht University The Netherlands e.carneirodeoliveira@uu.nl Hieke Keuning Utrecht University The Netherlands h.w.keuning@uu.nl student requests and discussion topics, and e
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used in programming education. However, little research has explored their use in teaching and learning code refactoring. In this study, we use a grounded-theory approach to examine student-LLM conversations during code refactoring exercises. Our preliminary results show that students use LLM in various modes, such as requesting a refactoring for the entire program at once or discussing refactoring possibilities in long conversations. 2 Study Design We conducted an experiment with 19 CS students enrolled in the Software Engineering course at Utrecht University. Students worked individually for one hour on code refactoring exercises, with optional assistance of ChatGPT. We designed three C# programming exercises that are functionally correct, but contain a number of code quality issues. The students’ task was to refactor code to resolve these issues - e.g. by using a design pattern or applying objectoriented design principles. We collected students’ solutions, their conversations with ChatGPT, and their survey responses on perceptions of ChatGPT’s use for the task. Our dataset consists of 41 student-LLM conversations for 3 exercises from 16 students—not all students tried each exercise or used ChatGPT. We have a total of 318 interactions to analyze. We are using a grounded-theory approach, in which all authors participate in the coding process.

papers.title: ScrumQuest Software Engineering Educational Tool: Teaching Planning in Scrum
papers.authors: HZ University of Applied Sciences Middelburg, To balance experience differences in the team, During sprint planning, As the sprint progresses
papers.abstract: Agile methodologies like Scrum are vital in software engineering (SE) education but can be complex for students. Especially, planning backlog items during a sprint turns out to be challenging. Our research develops and assesses a web-based educational tool, ScrumQuest, aimed at aiding first-year SE students in mastering Scrum practices with an emphasis on effective planning. Addressing a previous gap in Scrum educational tools, ScrumQuest also includes a unique and novel feature that provides automated feedback on sprint backlog activities to enhance student guidance. Evaluation involving 21 first-year SE university students indicated a positive experience with ScrumQuest, highlighting enhanced engagement and improved usage of sprint backlogs. Students found ScrumQuest easier to use than GitHub Projects, which served as a baseline in the study. In addition to developing and evaluating a novel Scrum educational tool, we contribute to design-science research by providing validated functional requirements within this context. We explain our research and demonstrate ScrumQuest’s practical relevance in Software Engineering education. Backlog Feedback (3) Sprint 1 Help Finish sprint Week 1 Monday Luke Joshua

papers.title: Adding Context to Automated Vulnerability Detection for
papers.authors: Maastricht University Maastricht, Maastricht University Maastricht, Maastricht University Maastricht, Maastricht University Maastricht
papers.abstract: Considering the recent developments in the fiel of generative AI, large language models (LLMs) can be leveraged to enhance static application security testing (SAST) tools and teaching about this topic. These models provide contextual information about identified vulnerabilities which can help students to differentiate genuine issues from false alarms while learning about software security. The approach includes analyzing vulnerabilities in android applications using SAST tools, clustering related code functionalities, and generating multi-level summaries for detected vulnerabilities. The process employs advanced clustering techniques and consensusbuilding methods to ensure accuracy. 2 We propose a solution that incorporates a large language model (LLM) to provide more context around reported vulnerabilities, currently utilizing the freely accessible version of ChatGPT for this purpose. This additional information helps students understand what distinguishes a real vulnerability from a false positive, and thus improves the learning experience. Our software pipeline includes a vulnerability analysis, followed by a parsing step that prepares for a clustering of the source code. The purpose of clustering is grouping program functionalities that operate on the same aspect of the program, e.g. GUI or storage, and then associate each detected vulnerability with one of the identified clusters. Once the clusters are identified, a textual summary is generated for each cluster that contains at least one vulnerability, along with summaries for the classes and methods contained in the cluster. The poster presents details on our approach, depicting the different steps of the software pipeline, and elaborating on how each of these works in detail. In addition, thoughts are presented on how to integrate the tool into teaching about software security.

papers.title: Fostering Computational Thinking in Elementary Mathematics Instruction and Learning with the Support of Large Language Models
papers.authors: Emma S. Ylagan Heena P. Parekh Malisha Das∗ Mai Dahshan University of Virginia School of Data Science Charlottesville, Virginia, USA xuu6qc@virginia.edu University of Virginia Department of Computer S
papers.abstract: Computational thinking (CT) integration in elementary mathematics engages young learners in the decomposition of complex problems and the construction of iterative approaches to mathematical thinking. To effectively integrate MATH+CT, we need to build teachers’ capacity in developing knowledge of CT concepts and creating Math+CT activities. This can positively influence students’ mathematical outcomes and their readiness for computer science (CS) in middle and high school. Although various professional development programs aim to build teachers’ CT knowledge, limited research exists on how teachers apply this knowledge to classroom-based Math+CT activities. Simultaneously, the rapid improvement of large Language Models (LLMs) creates a catalyst for building an innovative resource space to support elementary teachers’ integration of MATH+CT in their existing school or district curriculum. In this poster, we present a tool that leverages LLMs to support teachers in creating Scratch programs designed to explore and deepen students’ understanding of mathematical concepts. 1 Figure 1: Tool’s Pipeline for Generating Scratch Projects Using LLMs LLMs can play an important role in helping teachers integrate CT into mathematics teaching and learning in a variety of ways. With enhanced natural language understanding and notable improvements in problem solving abilities, LLMs hold great potential and promise to transform K-12 education [3]. They can provide innovative tools that help teach and learn, including but not limited to the generation of different varieties of math problems that improve CT, the creation of integrated MATH+CT activities and lesson plans, and automatic grading. In this poster, we present a web-based tool (Figure 1) that uses LLMs to generate MATH + CT activities by creating Scratch programs. Teachers enter a prompt through the tool’s web interface, which is sent to OpenAI API to generate the corresponding pseudocode, which describes the steps needed to create the program. This pseudocode is then used to generate a JSON file, ensuring explicit instructions about the Scratch blocks and logic so the resulting file is correct and functional. Finally, the JSON file is packaged as an SB3 file, along with any other supporting files, and sent back to the web interface as a downloadable link for use in Scratch.

papers.title: CyberQuest: An Interactive Web-Based Cybersecurity Platform
papers.authors: Department of Computer Science, Department of Computer Science, Department of Computer Science
papers.abstract: web-based platform, CyberQuest, which provides a safe sandbox environment, suitable helper tools, and specialized applications for teaching cybersecurity in the classroom. Feedback from educators and students alike was very positive, indicating the potential of the tool for effective classroom teaching. CyberQuest is freely available at https://cyberquest.ch and only requires a valid email address to access. It contains user and classroom management functionality that allows teachers to set up an isolated instance for their class. CyberQuest can be used in class as a complement to theoretical instruction phases, but our lessons also allow for a more autodidactic approach. We introduce a learning platform to teach cybersecurity topics in an interactive way to a K–12 audience. The platform targets cybersecurity novices and is entirely browser-based, making using it in class as simple as possible. It consists of two main components: a lesson center and a small mock social media network. The lesson center introduces students to basic concepts such as HTTP status codes and cookies, and asks them to carry out simple tasks within the social media network. Furthermore, students can look behind the curtains to see what kind of data is generated through interactions with the network. The ultimate goal is to “hack” into the social media network and impersonate a different user. Our system is designed in a modular way, so the social media network can be exchanged for a different “target application,” such as an email client or a chat application. It can thus be used to teach a wide range of security topics, while mimicking real-world settings. 2

papers.abstract: In addition to achieving learning outcomes, project-based learning (PBL) in groups is known to foster communications, team building, collaboration, and leadership skills, all essential for computer scientists in the workforce. Academic risk-taking, enabling students to attempt more complex problems and challenging projects, is a valuable skill for high academic achievement [7], making it a desirable skill for students in a fast-paced discipline. To explore the possibility of fostering academic risk-taking in PBL as a valuable skill for computer scientists, we focused on the impact of scaffolding to improve the PBL outcomes for diverse learners and its impact on risk-taking. We report on our initial findings and navigating grade-related risks, incentives, and timing constraints.

papers.title: Investigating the Impact of a Mentoring Program for Computer
papers.authors: Science Students with Disabilities Rebecca Robinson rebecca.robinson@monash.edu Department of Human Centred Computing Monash University Clayton, Victoria, Australia
papers.abstract: enhancing their engagement, fostering a sense of well-being, and improving their academic performance? We investigate the impact of a faculty-led mentoring program designed to support computer science students with disabilities. Grounded in existing literature that highlights the challenges these students face, including lower rates of retention and a reduced sense of belonging at university, the program provides individualized mentoring to address these issues. Data from an anonymous survey of program participants revealed the majority perceived it as providing benefits to their academic performance, sense of wellbeing, and sense of belonging at university. Despite the small sample size of eight students, the findings demonstrate potential for mentoring programs to enhance inclusivity and equity in STEM education. The results contribute to the growing body of research advocating for structured, proactive support systems for students with disabilities in higher education. 2 The program pairs teaching staff with students who are registered with disability services, providing one-on-one instruction tailored to individual needs. Mentors receive training in inclusive teaching practices and mental health support. Flexible, proactive engagement strategies are adopted when inviting students to participate. An anonymous 21 question survey with a mix of Likert-scale, multiple choice, and open-ended questions was delivered to participants to obtain information about level of engagement and student perceptions of the program’s impact. Responses were received from only eight students, however they highlighted benefits across several areas: • Improvements in academic performance (e.g., “Without the mentoring sessions, I would have most likely failed my unit.") • Increased sense of belonging (e.g., “It made me feel supported and helped by the school.") Students described how the structured nature of the mentoring helped them stay motivated and engaged with coursework. Challenges were also identified, pointing to potential areas for improvement, such as more flexible session formats and alternative communication strategies for students who struggle with self-advocacy. The findings, while based on a limited dataset, reinforce the importance of proactive, personalized support systems for students with disabilities in CS education. The poster will outline recommendations for refining and scaling such programs, including strategies to improve accessibility, increase participation, and enhance institutional support. We hope the poster session can lead to broader discussions about promoting equity and inclusion for students with disabilities in STEM fields, and how universities can move beyond passive accommodations toward active, structured support systems.

papers.title: Tracking the Progression of Errors Across Successive CS1 Code Submissions
papers.authors: Zhixian Christopher Liding Georgia Institute of Technology Atlanta, USA zliding3@gatech.edu Nimisha Roy Georgia Institute of Technology Atlanta, USA nroy9@gatech.edu Rodrigo Borela Georgia Institute o
papers.abstract: Understanding the debugging process of novice programmers as they iteratively solve coding challenges is essential for developing intelligent tutoring systems that address gaps in comprehension and procedural coding skills. This poster presents a framework for systematically analyzing student coding attempts using large language models (LLMs) to identify syntactical, conceptual, and strategic errors. This study investigates 346 coding attempts for three live-coding challenges in a CS1 course, tracking the progression of errors over successive submissions. Preliminary results indicate that among students who attempted the challenges at least ten times, syntactical errors decrease more rapidly within the first ten attempts compared to conceptual or strategic errors. Although students effectively resolve syntax issues early in the debugging process, higher-level conceptual and strategic errors persist, suggesting the need for targeted instructional support at this stage. Figure 1: Average Number of Errors Identified Per Submission prompt engineered with few-shot learning to identify errors. The model classified each error into syntactical, conceptual, and strategic categories using the framework introduced in [2] to reveal the low- or high-level nature of code errors. From three coding quizzes, 346 out of 856 submissions were considered from students who required at least ten attempts to solve a question, representing the bottom performing 15% of students when ranked by the number of attempts. Referring to Figure 1, the incidence of conceptual and strategic errors remained fairly constant across the first ten attempts, indicating minimal progress in addressing these higher-level misconceptions. In contrast, the incidence of syntactical errors dropped significantly within the first ten attempts, from 0.89 syntactical errors per submission to a minimum of 0.24. Thus, more effort was placed on resolving syntactical errors early in the debugging process. Given that the mean interval between the initial and the tenth attempts was 9.9 minutes, students typically spent ten minutes refining syntax without recognizing that their fundamental misunderstandings and strategic mistakes were the main obstacles to solving the problem successfully. These initial findings lay the foundation for our ongoing research into a key question: should LLM-generated feedback prioritize accelerating syntactical corrections, even when students are not on the correct path, or should higher-level logical errors be addressed earlier in the debugging process? As we continue this work, our goal is to refine these interventions to enhance learning and optimize the role of GenAI-driven feedback in the debugging process.

papers.title: Implementing Competency-Based Grading in a Large CS Course
papers.authors: Computer Science McGill University Montreal, Canada Institutional friction also emerged
papers.abstract: Traditional grading prioritizes point accumulation over mastery[3, 7], reinforcing strategies that hinder deep understanding. In large introductory courses, it can increase stress and inequities, particularly for students from diverse backgrounds [1, 2]. Competency-based grading (CBG) addresses these issues by focusing on mastery and providing multiple opportunities for improvement [4, 6]. Studies suggest CBG improves fairness, motivation, and transparency while reducing stress [5, 8], yet its implementation in large CS courses remains underexplored. We present the implementation of CBG in a 400+ student introductory CS course. Unlike traditional grading, CBG evaluates students on structured competency levels, with multiple opportunities to demonstrate understanding. Challenges included student resistance, grading misconceptions, and institutional hurdles. We outline the CBG structure, student responses, and key challenges, along with refinements to improve clarity and engagement. By ITiCSE 2025, preliminary survey data on engagement and motivation will offer insights into its effectiveness. 2

papers.title: StoryStudio: Enhancing Data Science Education with Explainable, Narrative-Driven Storytelling
papers.authors: Ryan Henry The University of Alabama Department of Computer Science Tuscaloosa, Alabama, USA rwhenry1@crimson.ua.edu Taha Hassan The University of Alabama Department of Computer Science Tuscaloosa, Al
papers.abstract: Data storytelling is essential in data science education but often lacks structured guidance. While students learn visualization and modeling, existing AI tools primarily generate stories automatically rather than teaching narrative construction. Few tools integrate storytelling with Jupyter Notebooks, and those that do focus on code generation rather than user-driven storytelling. StoryStudio bridges this gap by integrating with JupyterHub, allowing users to export figures and code into an interactive storytelling interface. It supports figure organization, AI-assisted insight extraction, and structured narrative generation using seven storytelling patterns. Unlike automated tools, Story Studio emphasizes active learning, helping students craft and refine their own data narratives. This poster will showcase Story Studio’s role in enhancing visual literacy and data communication in data science education. Figure 1: StoryStudio features a Jupyter-supported (left) web application for storyboarding and explainable, narrativedriven data storytelling (right). choice of story, rather than relying solely on AI-generated content. Figure 1 illustrates key features of StoryStudio. The objective of StoryStudio is to empower data science educators in the following three ways. First, StoryStudio allows users to arrange their visualizations in a storyboard to explore different story structures. Second, it supports AI-assisted data insight extraction, where visualizations and their associated code are processed using GPT-4o to generate rich descriptions. Third, it arranges these insights into narratives and stories, allowing users (or AI) to select from seven narrative patterns: (1) Time-Based Progressions, (2) Overview to Detail, (3) Cause and Effect, (4) Workflow/Process, (5) Comparison First/Insight Later, (6) Highlight Change/Impact, and (7) Build a Narrative. By focusing on user-driven storytelling, structured learning, and AI-assisted analysis, Story Studio offers a unique approach to teaching data literacy and communication. It also promises to bridges the gap between technical analysis and effective storytelling in data science education. Our poster will detail the results of a pilot empirical investigation (N=10) to evaluate the effectiveness of StoryStudio in crafting data stories.

papers.title: Supporting Teaching and Learning Computational Thinking Skills with Generative AI in Computing Education
papers.authors: Utrecht University Utrecht, CT skills
papers.abstract: Computational thinking (CT) skills allow us to achieve goals in a computation-driven world. Activities such as programming both benefit from and help improve CT skills, like abstraction and decomposition. Generative AI (GenAI) could be useful in developing CT skills. However, it could also change how we learn to program and which skills are more important. We aim to understand how GenAI can support the learning of CT skills in the context of computing education. 2 In this work, we consider CT to be a set of skills that includes decomposition, abstraction, algorithm design, generalization, and evaluation. For a detailed description of CT skills, see Selby [9]. There are many interventions aimed at developing CT skills [4], one of which is the use of Bebras tasks. Bebras1 is an initiative that aims to promote CT by presenting short tasks that require only general knowledge to solve but that are connected to computer science concepts [3]. Questions in Bebras tasks can be multiplechoice, open-ended, or interactive. Each year, educators worldwide collaborate to propose and approve hundreds of new tasks, which can later be adapted to different languages and pedagogical needs. Bebras tasks have been investigated as a way of measuring CT [11]. However, considering only the final answers may be insufficient to get a full picture of CT achievement. A think-aloud study on Bebras by de Jong et al. [5] found that analyzing the problem-solving process is important when assessing CT skills. GenAI is expected to influence many aspects of computing education, offering opportunities like timely feedback and explanations, as well as new types of learning activities. However, it also carries risks, such as overreliance, confusion, and plagiarism [7]. For example, LLMs can generate complete solutions to introductory programming exercises from just problem statements. In a paper about researching the use of GenAI in improving problem planning skills, Rivera et al. [8] describe a workflow that allows students to practice with an LLM-based tool. Good planning can help with organizing one’s thoughts and strategy when dealing with programming tasks. In their study, an LLM generates code from a student plan. The code is evaluated with automated tests and the results are shown to the student as feedback [8]. Planning can be seen as a complex activity involving many CT skills, like decomposition, abstraction, and algorithmic thinking. In a study on Bebras and GenAI, Bellettini et al. [2] analyzed the performance of an LLM in solving Bebras tasks. They found that the LLM answered only about one-third of the questions correctly, despite the seemingly high coherence and fluency of the responses.

papers.authors: University of Trento Trento
papers.abstract: 2 Computer Science Curricula 2023 identifies Society, Ethics, and Profession competencies essential to all computing topics and calls for their integration. However, limited research addresses faculty perspectives on developing these competencies. My PhD explores how educators acquire, refine, and implement SEP competencies, bridging the gap between ideal teaching and practice. The concept of “competency” has been widely debated across academic and professional domains, without universal consensus on its nature and definition. Its meaning has changed over time, contexts, languages, and regions, leading to many interpretations [13, 14]. Key distinctions between related words are needed to establish a common ground for a debate: Competence: A performance measure, a standard to meet in specific functions; Competency:The behavior(s) supporting an area of work; Competences: extends competence to perform a job well; Competencies: extends competency, the attributes underpinning a behavior. These distinctions distinguish job requirements from individual attributes that enable their fulfillment. [1, 8, 13, 17]

papers.abstract: I investigate the identification, explanation and treatment of common conceptual problems of students in introductory programming courses about control flow while reading code. In previous work I have identified and quantified several difficulties with control flow structures. The ultimate goal for my thesis is to develop a taxonomy, a concept inventory and effective educational methods for control flow concepts using methods of active learning and threshold concepts. These then can help more students to master the fundamental concepts of CS0 and CS1. 2 As this area has such a high importance for novice CS learners I aim my research at advancing and structuring the discovery of underlying conceptual problems, creating reliable and valid assessment tools and the development of effective educational material. For the sake of a clear scope I focus on the concept of control flow as it is a basic concept usually expected to be understood by students after an introductory course, but challenging enough for many students to fall short on it. The ultimate goal for my thesis is to develop a concept inventory and effective educational methods for control flow concepts.

papers.abstract: Challenge-Based Learning (CBL) is gaining popularity in higher education for Computer Science and Engineering degrees. It helps students develop essential skills in this rapidly-changing world such as collaboration, communication and critical thinking. However, designing and implementing CBL courses requires substantial effort and comes with various constraints. Universities often lack the ideal conditions and necessary resources, and there are no clear guidelines for developing flexible CBL courses. This research aims to explore the factors influencing CBL course structures and propose a scaffold adaptable to different environments. The goal is to make CBL more flexible, less dependent on costs and resources, and more widely adopted in higher education. 2

papers.title: Validated Assessment in Data Systems Education: A SQL
papers.authors: Empirical Study André V. R. P. Nascimento CESAR - Recife Center for Advanced Studies and Systems Recife, Pernambuco, Brazil andreviniciusnascimento@gmail.com prominent theme in Data Systems Education.
papers.abstract: Research on SQL education lacks validated assessment tools that ensure reliable and unbiased results. This study aims to develop a rigorously validated instrument to assess students' conceptual understanding of SQL, offering a reliable resource for research in Data Systems Education. 2 Problem Statement Given the proven relevance of SQL for various sectors, students in higher education courses related to Computing are expected to demonstrate competence in SQL equivalent to the mastery observed in programming languages. However, studies indicate that students usually have difficulties learning SQL [11, 13], which prevents them from reaching an adequate level of proficiency [8]. These difficulties are exacerbated by the students' limited exposure to topics focused on Data Systems. Miedema et al. [9] highlight that curricula in Computer Science offer several disciplines focused on programming, but this same emphasis is not given to Data Systems, which, in most cases, offer only one introductory discipline. The medium-term consequence of this deficiency is the gap between what students learn in academia and what the job market expects. The survey conducted by Miedema et al. [8] with industry professionals consistently indicated that newly hired graduates do not have practical experience with SQL and also have difficulties creating optimized queries for large databases. From the above, the importance of research aimed at improving the teaching and learning of SQL is evident, as well as the importance of studies that seek not only to verify but also to reduce the gap between academia and industry. Taipalus and Seppänen [14] carried out a systematic mapping study to give a broad overview of research related to teaching SQL and propagate teaching practices to educators. The results of the mapping provide a valuable overview of education research focused on SQL and highlight two important issues: (1) education research involving SQL is relatively scarce compared to the field of programming; and (2) there is a lack of replication studies. The authors emphasize that the lack of replication studies suggests that education research focused on SQL is not mature enough to distinguish between patterns and antipatterns. Thus, the following questions always persist: what is the best teaching approach to use? How to measure student learning? One solution that can help answer these questions is the adoption of validated assessment instruments, which can increase the reliability and value of the results produced by research.

papers.authors: An Entangled Computer Science Pedagogy Gaye Stephens School of Computer Science and Statistics Trinity College Dublin Ireland gaye.stephens@tcd.ie
papers.abstract: to place generic TE learning outcomes at a programme level with learning outcome specificity evolving through pedagogical alignment in CS disciplines. Understanding how ethical conceptions are used in real world CS design practices is a first step to specifying programme level learning outcomes and objectives. The importance of and challenges to incorporating technology ethics (TE) as a topic on computer science programmes has been established. Being mindful of the challenges, the research proposed here aims to explore the extent to which a serious game, SimEthica, pedagogically entangled within a CS programme is useful for cultivating ethical thinking in computer science students. There are many conceptions and traditions of ethical thought providing complimentary, overlapping and contradictory lenses. Three traditions of western ethical thought are aretaic e.g. virtue ethics concerning people’s character, non consequentialist e.g. deontology which considers what we ought to do and consequentialist e.g. utilitarianism concerning maximization of benefit and minimization of harm. Elements of these traditions can be found in CS ethical design practices. In [6] Reijers reviews, classifies and critically discusses existing practices, outlining their shortcomings and offering recommendations for improvements. Virtuous practice design (VPD) [7] is developed as a response to the recommendations. VPD arises from explication and synthesis of features from virtue ethics, technical practice, narrative technologies and philosophies of Paul Ricoeur [8]. It embeds deontological formalism within a virtue ethics based frame. Through many steps and stages and the use of narratives, VPD cultivates designers’ virtues. It provides means to scope and evaluate technical practices, understand perspectives and collaboratively and competitively balance alternatives and prescribe design changes. VPD is mainly a theoretical research contribution with limited practical tools in the form of an ethics canvas [9]. There is opportunity to explore the extent to which VPD could usefully be embedded in a pedagogically entangled game to cultivate students’ ethical thinking.

papers.title: Love, Learning, and Computing Education
papers.authors: Amy J. Ko, University of Washington Seattle
papers.abstract: We live in a world that is increasingly full of hate, cruelty, and violence. These cultural forces are destabilizing schools, colleges, universities, libraries, and other places of informal learning, and every learner, teacher, and leader in them, threatening education and democracy in the U.S. and worldwide. What is our role, as computing educators and scholars, in resisting this hate? In this talk, I argue for love. A kind of love that shows up not as an abstraction in our values, but in the concrete ways that we teach computing, in the questions we ask about learning computing, in the technologies we create to support computing education, and in what we choose to teach about computing. To make this case, I examine my own experiences with love in computing education and then offer a conception of love in computing education. I then deconstruct some of the fundamental tensions between love, computing, and computing education culture. I end with several examples of loving computing education from scholars in our community, each showing us how we might reimagine our teaching, research, and institutions around love. Through this transformation, I hope we might inspire a generation of youth to help create both loving uses of computing, a loving society more broadly, and perhaps a more loving scholarly community for ourselves. papers.abstract: Keywords CS educators teach programming. Generative AI tools can program. So we’re clearly wasting our time teaching CS to students in the AI era, right? There’s no need for junior programmers, enrollments are dropping, and we should all plan to be plumbers or apple farmers. Or perhaps there is a chance to use the AI crisis as an opportunity to do make some much-needed changes to our programs. For in computing education, as in so many other topics, AI is not an answer, it is only an accelerant. For topics with sound foundations, it’s a boon, reducing friction and toil. For topics with long-standing shortcomings, it’s adding fuel to the fire. In this talk I’ll give some industry perspective, identify what seems outdated in CS and SE pedagogy, and try to sketch out some more fruitful directions for revision to our assignments, classes, and overall curricula. In this work, we extend these efforts by creating additional games centered on designing for individuals with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism. We used all three games in an Introduction to HCI course to provide students with interactive experiences that illustrate both the impact of inaccessible software on neurodivergent users and the value of accessible solutions. We aim to address the following research questions: RQ1: Does playing accessibility games increase students’ awareness of software accessibility for neurodivergent users? RQ2: Do accessibility-focused games effectively teach students about the practical challenges and solutions related to inaccessible software for neurodivergent users? RQ3: How do students perceive and perform in accessibility-focused games designed to teach inclusive design for neurodivergent users? While accessibility education for designing for people with disabilities has become more common in university computing classrooms, instruction focused on designing for neurodivergent users remains limited. In this work, we developed accessibility games to teach students about accessible design for neurodivergent users and evaluated them on 43 students in a university Human-Computer Interaction course. Students found the games to be engaging and learned about designing accessible solutions for neurodivergent individuals. Some challenges emerged in terms of making the games more universal across languages and cultures.

ACM, New York, NY, USA, 7 pages. https://doi.org/10. 1145/3770762.3772617 Background: Prior research on a culturally responsive summer computer science (CS) program for high school students found that demographic disparities remained in students’ likelihood of pursuing CS. Purpose: This study investigates why such disparities might have emerged by exploring factors that may differentially influence students’ motivation to pursue CS. We center students’ perspectives and aim to offer recommendations for educators to create equitable and impactful CS learning experiences. Methods: We interviewed nine high school students from the summer CS program and qualitatively analyzed their responses using a theoretical framework that identifies factors that shape students’ motivation to pursue CS. Findings: Our analysis identified five potential influences on our participants’ motivation including: perceptions of their own and others’ CS ability, concerns about the climate in CS environments, stereotypes about computer scientists, competing interests in other careers, and narrow understandings about what CS can be used for. Implications: By examining students’ experiences in a culturally responsive program, this study contributes to understanding both the potential and the limits of such programs. papers.abstract: CCS Concepts This quasi-experimental study integrates a large language model (LLM) with expert qualitative analysis to examine how instructional design variations in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) shape collaboration in data-centric programming. We collected 73 team transcripts from two contrasting CSCL designs deployed across five course offerings: a closed-ended variant with prescribed solution paths and auto-graded milestones, and an openended variant supporting exploratory tasks with multiple valid paths. LLM annotation revealed statistically significant differences in knowledge co-construction patterns: the open-ended design yielded a higher proportion of utterances focused on developing a shared understanding of problems and solutions. Guided by these quantitative results, human experts conducted qualitative coding that confirmed and enriched these findings, showing how openended tasks fostered elaborative solution negotiation while closedended structures promoted non-elaborative exchanges. Our contributions are: (1) instructional insights for data science education, demonstrating how open-ended CSCL designs better support collaborative sense-making essential for real-world data science projects; and (2) a documented workflow for human-LLM co-evaluation, providing the methodological detail necessary for others to replicate our process and apply it to future studies. • Social and professional topics → Adult education; Computing education; • Applied computing → Collaborative learning.

Partnering with Community College Faculty to Co-Design Intelligent Tutoring Systems for Cybersecurity Workforce Training. In Proceedings of the 57th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V.1 (SIGCSE TS 2026), February 18–21, 2026, St. Louis, MO, USA. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 7 pages. https://doi.org/10. 1145/3770762.3772524 This experience report describes a partnership between community college faculty and learning scientists to co-design Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) addressing challenges in cybersecurity workforce training. Our co-design approach combined collaborative reflection on student difficulties from prior course offerings with systematic curricular analysis to identify high-impact intervention points. We targeted two challenge areas: strengthening students’ ability to contrast key cybersecurity taxonomies, and providing realistic hands-on training without costly infrastructure. The resulting ITSs include: one employing exercises that scaffold comparison of conceptual categories, and another using lightweight simulations to provide experiential learning while circumventing typical cost and time overhead. Both systems incorporate instructional principles grounded in learning science research, including evidence-based features associated with ITS efficacy such as timely hints and feedback. Through iterative classroom deployment and refinement—including adding task-loop adaptivity to offer repeated practice until mastery—we observed encouraging learning outcomes, alongside insights into mitigating “gaming the system” behaviors. We detail our co-design process and formative evaluations—procedures, outcomes, and cautious interpretation due to the limited number of consented learners—and share lessons learned to inform scalable ITS development for cybersecurity workforce training in resource-constrained settings.

papers.title: Fighting Fire with Fire: LLM-Assisted Grading of Handwritten CS Assessments
papers.authors: Irvine Irvine, University of California, Irvine Irvine, University of California, Irvine Irvine, Irvine Irvine, University of California, Irvine Irvine
papers.abstract: Keywords Widespread student adoption of large language models (LLMs) has prompted many CS instructors to assign greater weight to handwritten, proctored assessments. However, this approach struggles to scale as class sizes outpace course staff resources. To address this challenge, our study explores LLM-assisted grading to reduce required grading time. While prior work has emphasized tool accuracy, we evaluate both time and accuracy by comparing outcomes when course staff use an LLM-assisted grader versus Gradescope. We also incorporate a mixed-methods analysis of student and staff perceptions. In a CS1 course of 166 students supported by four teaching assistants (TAs), we observed that LLM-assisted grading reduced overall grading time by 40% compared to Gradescope, with time savings of 48% for exams and 25% for quizzes. Across all assessments, short answer questions showed a 46% time improvement, and free response questions showed a 37% time improvement. In terms of accuracy, accepted regrade requests increased negligibly from 0.1% to 0.5% across three exams and six quizzes. Students were generally neutral about LLM-assisted grading, but stressed the value of TA feedback and oversight. Meanwhile, TAs expressed positive sentiments towards the tool, tempered by concerns of skewed perceptions of students caused by the tool. Overall, these findings indicate that LLM-assisted grading can greatly reduce grading time, with only minor accuracy trade-offs that can be mitigated. As a result, LLM-assisted grading emerges as a promising approach for enhancing grading efficiency in CS courses, meriting further exploration for broader adoption. papers.abstract: Keywords In introductory programming courses, students increasingly submit code generated by large language models (LLMs) instead of solving problems independently. This growing reliance raises concerns about students’ development of programming skills. To reduce the overreliance and promote independent problem solving, we propose an explainable detection framework that predicts whether a code submission was generated by an LLM and provides an explanation for its prediction. Such explanations are crucial in educational settings, where transparency and feedback are essential. To support this, we construct a dataset of student-written and LLM-generated code, paired with explanations automatically produced using GPT-4o. We finetune several code-specialized LLMs using both binary labels (student-written or LLM-generated) and explanations. The resulting models achieve over 99% accuracy and generate informative explanations aligned with their predictions, both validated by human instructors. We also apply our detector to past programming course data, revealing a sharp increase in LLM-generated submissions—from nearly 0% in 2022A to over 40% in 2024A. We conclude with a discussion of false positives and suggest how explainable detection can be responsibly deployed in programming courses. papers.abstract: Ethics instruction, as required for ABET-accreditation and recommended by the ACM/IEEE-CS/AAAI curricular guidelines, is an important element of the undergraduate computer science (CS) curriculum. Recent papers that analyze the proportion of programs offering CS ethics education focus on specific types of programs, such as top-ranked programs, programs at R1 institutions under the Carnegie Classification, and/or ABET-accredited programs. This leaves out a large portion of CS programs that may fall under none of those categories, including many small colleges. In this paper, we analyze a true random sample of all 4-year Bachelor’s, Public or Private Not-For-Profit CS programs in the United States (U.S.) to assess the extent to which the previous data holds true across the full spectrum of U.S. colleges and universities. Using a systematic approach, we look at which CS programs require CS ethics instruction, whether as a standalone course or integrated into other courses. In addition, we break down the data by categorization to replicate previous studies and place our data in conversation with those. We found that 55% of all U.S. CS programs require CS ethics in some capacity. Additionally, we found ABET-accreditation and Carnegie research classification to be a major driver toward programs requiring ethics instruction in the U.S.

papers.authors: Learning Functional Programming Jacob Bell, Grinnell College Grinnell, USA Salyan Karki, Grinnell College Grinnell, USA William Pitchford, Grinnell College Grinnell, USA Anna Deschamps Eva Kapoor, Grinnell College Grinnell, Grinnell College Grinnell, Grinnell College Grinnell, USA Elene Sturua, Grinnell College Grinnell, Grinnell College Grinnell, USA Charles Wade, Grinnell College Grinnell, USA Samuel A. Rebelsky, Grinnell College Grinnell, USA Finally
papers.abstract: Programming exercises are central to learning. Parsons Problems (PPs) ask students to arrange shuffled code blocks into correct order, emphasizing logic over syntax and enabling efficient assessment. Furthermore, by focusing on mastering logic rather than syntax, PPs reduce students’ cognitive load and provide a more direct mechanism for assessing students. However, most PPs and environments for building PPs emphasize a sequential model, where code chunks primarily revolve around line-based programming. What if we want students to master other kinds of sequencing? For example, most modern languages and frameworks now support functional programming, a model in which sequencing is often achieved by nesting expressions rather than ordering statements. In addition, functional approaches also permit higher-order operations—such as mapping, filtering, and reducing—in which the programmer may best understand the work as being done in parallel. Can we reframe PPs to teach such concepts? We address these problems by introducing Nested-Block PPs, composed of blocks in which students drag and drop subexpressions into other expressions. We then show the utility of this approach in developing functional programming problems. Our system also includes a code executor that can generate output and provide error messages, which permits students to receive real-time feedback.

papers.title: Like Parsley in Greek Food:
papers.authors: Siddharth Bhaskar, University of Southern Denmark Odense
papers.abstract: The fact is that algebraic geometers do make great programmers, but not because of their expertise in algebraic geometry. They make great programmers because of the depth of their mathematical sophistication. With regards to computer science, even as practiced in industry, Mathematics should not be understood as collection of topical prerequisites, but rather as an ambient conceptual framework. Unfortunately, mathematics requirements within computer science curricula are almost universally based on the idea of covering prerequisites. Even when it is explicitly noted that a role of mathematics is to convey a certain way of thinking, this is rarely exploited as a principled basis for course design. We consequently fail to impart mathematical sophistication to our students in a widespread and replicable way, and this in turn strongly inhibits our ability to teach the sort of high-level conceptual thinking particular to our discipline (sometimes called “the computational lens” or “computational thinking,” cf. [10, 11]). The problem is that mathematical sophistication and conceptual frameworks are vague whereas topics are satisfyingly concrete. My basic goal is to inject enough precision into these notions that course design actually becomes feasible. The predominant design philosophy behind most Discrete Mathematics (DM) courses is that of a recycling bin: a place where mathematical prerequisites with no other natural home can live out the rest of their days in peace. This fundamentally misunderstands the role of mathematics in computer science. Instead of being a collection of topical prerequisites, mathematics provides a conceptual framework enabling the sort of high-level computational thinking that a computer science bachelor’s degree is supposed to train. I argue that the field of mathematics in question can be profitably identified with elementary set theory, roughly, the theory of (naive) sets and relations with structural induction. I propose an alternate model of mathematics education in the computer science degree: a ‘DM1’ (and possibly DM2) course that receives as much importance as the CS1/2 sequence and are similarly foregrounded in the program of study.

papers.title: Understanding Software Engineering Practices and Tools in
papers.authors: Franklin W. Olin College of Engineering Needham, USA Ramzey Burdette, Franklin W. Olin College of Engineering Needham, USA Michelle Jarvie-Eggart Titilayo Oshinowo, Franklin W. Olin College of Engineering Needham, USA Stephanos Matsumoto, Michigan Technological University Houghton, Franklin W. Olin College of Engineering Needham
papers.abstract: Keywords Though software development has increasingly become a part of modern engineering practice, even outside of computing, we lack a sufficiently deep understanding of how engineers in many disciplines learn and use software engineering practices and tools (SEPTs). SEPTs include, but extend beyond, programming itself, consisting of practices (e.g., unit testing) and tools (e.g., version control software) that support the design, implementation, or maintenance of software. While many disciplines outside of computing teach programming in their undergraduate curricula, little is known about how these disciplines use, teach, or adopt SEPTs. We thus conducted an exploratory qualitative study on SEPTs among undergraduate students in mechanical engineering (ME), one of the largest engineering disciplines in the US. Specifically, we explored two research questions: (1) What SEPTs do undergraduate ME students use in their work? (2) What factors influence undergraduate ME students’ adoption of these SEPTs? We conducted and analyzed three unstructured interviews with ME students at different institutions, using the Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) as theoretical frameworks. Our results show that ME students’ SEPTs span relatively few SWEBOK areas, and are strongly influenced by course design, disciplinary context, and expected time/effort. These results suggest that with continued work in this area, we can likely gain and apply evidence-based insights to improve the teaching of SEPTs within ME in a way that is authentic to its disciplinary context. software engineering; mechanical engineering; practice; tools; undergraduate education; qualitative; interview; technology adoption

papers.abstract: Automated feedback generation plays a crucial role in enhancing personalized learning experiences in computer science education. Among different types of feedback, next-step hint feedback is particularly important, as it provides students with actionable steps to progress towards solving programming tasks. This study investigates how students interact with an AI-driven next-step hint system in an in-IDE learning environment. We gathered and analyzed a dataset from 34 students solving Kotlin tasks, containing detailed hint interaction logs. We applied process mining techniques and identified 16 common interaction scenarios. Semi-structured interviews with 6 students revealed strategies for managing unhelpful hints, such as adapting partial hints or modifying code to generate variations of the same hint. These findings, combined with our publicly available dataset, offer valuable opportunities for future research and provide key insights into student behavior, helping improve hint design for enhanced learning support.

papers.abstract: We report on the results of a year-long intervention aimed at introducing parallel and distributed computing (PDC) concepts in introductory computing courses. In contrast to other efforts, our approach uses “codeless” modules that incorporate visualizations, simulations, and demonstrations, all of which do not require a programming background, making them accessible to novice computing students. To measure the effectiveness of our strategy, we designed and administered a pre/posttest to an intervention group (𝑛 2 = 75) and compared it with a control group (𝑛 1 = 87). A suite of nonparametric tests demonstrate that our codeless modules have a substantial positive effect on teaching PDC concepts to introductory computing students.

papers.authors: University of Toronto Toronto, To address this, The module is designed to be lightweight, Our goal is to share a replicable
papers.abstract: We present the development of an asynchronous online module for teaching software documentation in an introductory software design course. Drawing on literature from industry practices and computing education, we designed a lightweight, self-paced module that introduces students to the principles of effective documentation. A central feature of the module is our ACCEU framework, which defines five key dimensions of documentation quality: accuracy, clarity, completeness, ease of use, and up-to-dateness. These dimensions are grounded in a synthesis of prior research and serve as a practical guide for students documenting both code and software projects. We describe the pedagogical motivations behind our design, the structure and content of the module, and initial student feedback. Our experience suggests that the module was well received by our students and met our goals. We conclude with recommendations for instructors interested in adopting or adapting our described approach.
