papers.title: From Confidence to Doubt: A Multi-year Analysis of Students’ Problem-Solving Attitudes in a CS2 Course
papers.authors: Zhikai Gao Matthew Zahn, Western Carolina University Cullowhee, North Carolina State University Raleigh, USA Collin Lynch Sarah Heckman, North Carolina State University Raleigh, North Carolina State University Raleigh, USA of generative AI, To address this gap, Using validated survey instruments
papers.abstract: In recent years, computer science (CS) education has undergone rapid change, first due to the shift to online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic, and more recently with the rise of generative AI (GenAI) tools. How these changes impact students’ learning habits and problem-solving attitude remains unknown. This paper presents a long-term analysis of attitudinal survey data from a CS2 course across eight semesters. Drawing on the Computing Attitudes Survey (CAS v4) and the Computer Science Attitudes (CSA) survey, we measure changes in seven constructs, including confidence, mindset, strategies, and motivation. We observe stable or positive shifts in earlier semesters, but sharp negative trends in Fall 2023 and Spring 2024—semesters coinciding with the widespread availability of Generative AI (GenAI) tools. These results highlight the urgent need for instructors to consider how new technologies shape not just students’ learning outcomes but their beliefs about their own ability to succeed in computing. 2 We have collected data from eight offerings (Fall 2020 - Spring 2024) of an undergraduate CS2 software development fundamentals course at an R1 university in the United States and approved by their IRB. This course prohibited the use of GenAI tools on all assignments and coursework. While this does not mean that students did not use these resources, every semester the syllabus clearly outlined that GenAI was prohibited.

papers.title: Situating LLMs in Time: A Visual Tool for Teaching the History and Architecture of Modern NLP
papers.authors: United States, United States, To address this gap, LLM Timeline, Starting from the Transformer
papers.abstract: Understanding the history of technology is essential to teaching computer science, not just how systems work, but how we got there. This is more true in the rapid evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs), whose development since 2017 offers a rich, branching narrative of innovation and adaptation. To support history-aware computing education, we introduce an interactive visual timeline that traces the lineage of LLMs, and different techniques within, from the foundational "Attention is All You Need" paper through major model families and research directions. Our tool, LLM Timeline, is organized as a top-down graph with color coded branches that represent various architectures and approaches such as DecoderOnly, Encoder-Only, Mixture-of-Experts, Multimodal, and much more, allowing students to explore not only technical contributions but also the intellectual lineage of modern AI. 2 Related Works Interactive visualizations have become powerful tools in computing education, helping learners build intuition about abstract concepts. Examples like TensorFlow Playground [10] illustrate neural network training through real-time manipulation, while Distil.pub [11] introduce interactive scientific papers that blend narrative, code, and dynamic visuals to explain deep learning phenomena. In NLP education, Jay Alammar’s illustrated Transformer [2] and The Annotated Transformer [15] offer accessible, visual walkthroughs of the Transformer architecture. Yet, they all focus primarily on how a single model works, and not how the field evolved. Broader platforms such as Papers with Code and Hugging Face Model Hub connect research papers to code and benchmarks, but prioritize utility over historical or conceptual context. Our work addresses this gap by explicit mapping of the intellectual lineage of large language models. By organizing influential papers into topical branches, and linking each to it’s predecessors, the LLM Timeline helps students see AI progress as a coherent narrative of innovations. This aligns with growing calls in CS education to teach not just technical skills, but the historical reasoning and design trade-offs behind modern systems.

papers.title: Preparing Graduate Teaching Assistants with Structured Orientation and AI-Simulated Students
papers.authors: Houyame Lkhider, Purdue University West Lafayette, Purdue University West Lafayette, USA Ethan Dickey Andres Bejarano, Purdue University West Lafayette, Purdue University West Lafayette
papers.abstract: 1 Graduate Teaching Assistants (GTAs) support a substantial share of undergraduate computing instruction, yet many enter their roles with limited preparation and opportunity for feedback. To create greater consistency and scalability, we implemented a redesigned GTA training at a large R1 university that integrates multiday workshops, asynchronous modules, and AI-simulated student communication practice. The model emphasizes professional communication, classroom management, and equitable teaching practices while generating diagnostic data to inform ongoing instructional coaching. In two cohorts (n = 266), GTAs who completed workshops and simulations reported higher confidence and demonstrated stronger communication and adaptability performance than peers who completed online modules alone. These findings suggest that a structured, evidence-based orientation supported by AI student simulations shows promise for scalable implementation across large programs while maintaining pedagogical depth. Graduate Teaching Assistants (GTAs) are integral to undergraduate computing education: staffing laboratories and office hours, grading and sometimes creating assignments, responding to online discussion forum posts, and providing one-to-one academic support that shapes students’ early experiences. However, preparation for these roles often varies widely. At a large R1 university, more than 250 GTAs are assigned annually in the computer science department, entering with varied experience levels and pedagogical training. Historically, this inconsistency produced uneven communication practices, uncertainty in classroom management, and elevated faculty concerns about policy enforcement. Such challenges echo findings in computing-education research: fragmented training contributes to inconsistent pedagogy, elevated stress, and higher attrition among novice instructors [2, 4]. To address these gaps, our department of computer science redesigned its GTA orientation to establish a common baseline of expectations and measurable readiness indicators. The model integrates asynchronous modules, interactive workshops, and AIsimulated teaching practice to build confidence and professional judgment through iterative learning and feedback.

papers.title: A Data Structures Field Trip? Integrating a Library Visit into CS2
papers.authors: Stonehill College Easton
papers.abstract: While some existing research on teaching the relationship between theory and practice in data structures has relied on largescale programming projects [7], peer instruction [10] or more contextualized assignments [13], we explore an orthogonal approach: using class time to show the impact of theoretical computer science concepts in the real world beyond computing. This approach draws on the history of “unplugged” computer science activities [2], introducing key ideas from computer science to students without computers, which are popular with primary and secondary school teachers [1]. It is also particularly timely as generative AI has put pressure on computer science pedagogy to rely less on take-home programming assignments for student learning [9, 12]. To that end, we have begun integrating a one-session field trip to our campus library into our undergraduate data structures course. The objective of this trip is to showcase the way that the library itself functions as a data structure, the abstract data types that it implements and the time and space complexity tradeoffs at play in the storage and retrieval of physical library materials. Additionally, we use this activity as a first opportunity to introduce computer science students to information science concepts. Computer science students often struggle to understand the realworld implications of theoretical computer science. In our data structures course, we conducted an experimental activity taking students on a field trip to the school library in order to showcase the ways that the library functions as a data structure, and the algorithms that library staff employ to keep the library running smoothly. Here, we describe the design of four activities for data structures students at the library and encourage other courses to consider integrating real-world examples of data structures and algorithms into their courses.

papers.title: Translating Smart Content for Learning Python through Human-AI Collaboration
papers.authors: Mohammad Hassany Peter Brusilovsky, University of Pittsburgh Pittsburgh, University of Pittsburgh Pittsburgh, USA Jordan Barria-Pineda Isaac Alpizar-Chacon, University of Pittsburgh Pittsburgh, Utrecht University Utrecht, English text, In this paper
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present an approach that enables a broad re-use of English-authored smart learning content by translating it into other languages. To make it possible, we integrated translation functionalities directly into a smart content authoring system and engaging human-AI collaboration. The approach has been used to translate a large volume of worked examples and completion problems in Python from English to Spanish. The translated content has been piloted in several universities in a Spanish-speaking country.

papers.title: A Statewide Analysis of Ethics and Social Impact in the CS
papers.authors: Berkeley Berkeley, University of California, Berkeley Berkeley, CS education, CS teacher licensure, In this emergent work
papers.abstract: The landscape of K-12 computer science (CS) teacher credentialing in the United States is highly variable across pathways and curricula [9]. Scholars in CS education have called for more critical, justiceoriented approaches, particularly in teacher preparation [8, 13]. While the calls to do this work are apparent, it is less clear to what extent teachers in these programs are critically examining the social impacts and ethical considerations of computing. Our research question was: To what extent and in what ways do course descriptions in CS teacher credentialing programs address ethics and social impact? Our data collection focused on a single state with a clear credential pathway for CS. We examined all universities in that state offering a CS teacher credentialing program and compiled a dataset of their course titles, numbers, and descriptions. In total, we identified 89 courses across 18 universities. Further qualitative analysis demonstrated that the inclusion of ethics and social impact in course descriptions was uneven. Some courses highlighted the dual nature of CS as a tool for both innovation and oppression, while others made only brief mention of its social impact. This research highlights the need to examine the content of the CS curriculum for teacher credentialing candidates and the nature of how ethics and social impact are discussed.

papers.title: Blended Student Exchange Between the USA and EU: A Practical Approach to CS Education and Physical Computing
papers.authors: Northeastern Illinois University Chicago, German International School Mountain View, Karlsruhe University of Education Karlsruhe
papers.abstract: 1 This poster presents a practical model for transatlantic collaboration in computer science education through a blended mobility program between Karlsruhe University of Education (Germany) and Northeastern Illinois University (USA). The program funded by the European Union (Erasmus+) combines virtual and physical mobility phases, enabling students to participate in collaborative courses such as Physical Computing and Cybersecurity without interrupting their home semester. We share insights from the program’s first implementation cycle, including student feedback and preliminary data on learning outcomes. This model demonstrates how EU-US cooperation can effectively support practical, handson computer science courses in a blended learning environment. Our work highlights challenges and best practices for designing sustainable, international blended mobility programs in computer science teacher education, offering valuable implications for institutions seeking to foster global collaboration in computer science education. Blended mobility programs offer structured ways to foster international collaboration in higher education [7] while addressing logistical and financial barriers to full-semester exchanges. This poster presents a practical model developed between Karlsruhe University of Education (PHKA) and Northeastern Illinois University (NEIU), combining virtual and short-term physical phases in courses such as Physical Computing and Cybersecurity. Early feedback indicates that this format effectively supports collaborative, hands-on learning [3] within the computer science teacher education. For the SIGCSE community, this model demonstrates how global partnerships can be embedded into CS curricula, offering scalable, inclusive approaches to experiential learning and internationalization. 2

papers.title: Bridging Classroom and Industry: Student Perspectives on the Impact of CS Coursework on Internship Readiness
papers.authors: University Patchogue, New York, University Brooklyn, New York
papers.abstract: Internship experiences are valuable components of undergraduate computing programs, offering students the chance to apply classroom knowledge and skills in a real-world setting. In evaluating the computing curricula, an important question arises about which courses have the greatest impact on students’ preparedness for internships. Interested in getting student perceptions of course impact, we required students at our institution who completed computing internships, to submit a reflection paper which included a prompt about which courses they found most beneficial during their internship experience. These reflections were analyzed by tracking the frequency of specific course mentions and identifying common themes across responses. This work’s purpose was to determine how we could adjust our CS course content, sequences, and requirements to better serve students prior to them attaining internships. The findings revealed that while students saw value in nearly every course within the computing curriculum, certain courses stood out as being especially impactful. 2 • What courses that you completed towards your degree were beneficial to your internship work? • Explain how you applied the content from those courses to your internship.

papers.title: Sense of Community in an Asynchronous Online Degree Program
papers.authors: Dustin Jay Hooks Casey Fiesler Computer Science University of Colorado Boulder, CO, USA dustin.hooks@colorado.edu Information Science University of Colorado Boulder, CO, USA casey.fiesler@colorado.edu
papers.abstract: Students’ sense of community within educational environments can have a significant impact on the learning outcomes of those students. Fostering this type of connection can be challenging for online degree programs, particularly for asynchronous programs. Recognizing the potential benefits and improved student outcomes to be gained from a stronger student sense of community, we are conducting a survey study in an online Masters in Computer Science program in order to evaluate the current sense of community for the students and discover what factors could be leveraged to strengthen it. Preliminary pilot results indicate a lower sense of connectedness than learning in the program, which could lead one to assume a need to increase connectedness. However, these same preliminary results also suggest the importance of future work assessing student perspectives on the desirability of increasing connectedness.

papers.title: Co-designing and Implementing Critical Computing Lesson Plans with K-12 Teachers
papers.authors: Amber Hu Aman Yadav, University of Washington Seattle, Michigan State University East Lansing, In higher education
papers.abstract: As demand for K-12 computer science (CS) education grows, we argue that most students would be best served by CS classes that not only teach computational thinking/programming, but also challenge them to critically analyze the role of technology in society. One of the main barriers to implementing this in K-12 classrooms is a lack of research on how in-service CS teachers can integrate critical pedagogy into their school context and existing curricula. This poster presents results from a study to co-design lessons with current K-12 CS teachers to integrate critical perspectives into their classrooms. Teacher participants participated in a synchronous professional learning series in which we taught them critical computing content drawn from relevant books and frameworks. Following this, we collaborated with the teacher participants to design or modify lessons that engage their students in critical analysis, which the participants then implemented in their classrooms. Teachers were encouraged to include content relevant to their students and the communities they are a part of. We conducted thematic analysis of transcripts from the interviews, professional learning series, and co-design sessions. The resulting eight (8) themes demonstrate the challenges and opportunities inherent in integrating critical perspectives into K-12 computing education. In the long term, results from this work will inform future sociocultural content integration into K-12 CS courses (e.g. "ethics content"). 2 Study design 2.1 Co-design This study addresses the gap in K-12 critical computing education lesson implementations by co-designing lesson plans with in-service K-12 computing teachers. In the context of design thinking, co-design is a process of collaborative design, involving a group of participants with different stakeholder identities [13]. For this study, we facilitated instructional co-design, which is a process in which research participants are actively engaged in designing and guiding the process for creating curriculum [5]. 2.2

papers.title: Encouraging Student Use of AI in CS1:
papers.authors: Rethinking Content, IA USA
papers.abstract: that the traditional model of evaluating comprehension of computing concepts by having students write simple programs is no longer meaningful. It has been well documented that generative AI tools are capable of solving traditional CS1-level problems as effectively as beginner students. With the addition of this technology as part of the technological landscape, it is necessary to reconsider expectations for CS1 content as well as the pedagogical approaches we choose to adopt. This poster documents the experience teaching a recent course that encouraged students to use a generative AI tool while revisiting four pedagogical tools: Problem-Centric Instruction, Flipped Instruction, Competency Demonstrations and In-Person Code reviews. Not only can AI serve as a catalyst to rethink what it means for students to engage with introductory programming, it also provides an opportunity to revisit some of the pedagogical advancements that we should have been paying attention to all along. As with many technological advances, Generative AI has experienced hesitation and skepticism as practitioners wrestle with the scope and impact of the tool. There were early efforts to curtail the use of generative AI, equating it with cheating [2]. However, given the rapid advancement and pervasiveness of this technology, others have suggested that we embrace the technology and look for new ways to empower programmers [3]. These proponents view generative AI as an evolutionary step that continues the progression from machine language, to higher level languages and onward now to natural language [1]. Encouraging the use of this technology greatly reduces the instructional emphasis on syntax and allows us focus on other formative skills for novice computer scientists [4]. What does the new CS1 course look like when AI is added to the equation?

papers.title: Engaging Minority High School Students in AI-Enhanced
papers.authors: Tuskegee University Tuskegee, Tuskegee University Tuskegee, Tuskegee University Tuskegee
papers.abstract: CCS Concepts This study shares lessons learned from a culturally responsive program designed to broaden computer science (CS) participation and build foundational AI literacy among minority high school students from low-income communities. The program emphasized collaborative, project-based app design as a strategy to foster CS interest and develop AI literacy skills. The program included two phases: a one-month summer academy and a semester-long fall project. In the summer academy, 42 students engaged in MIT App Inventor programming, Agile software development, and AI lessons covering machine learning concepts and AI ethics. In the fall, 26 students continued in bi-weekly online Zoom meetings, collaboratively designing personally meaningful mobile app prototypes, such as a hair-care recommendation app for Black women and a mental-health support app for teenagers. Evaluation methods included surveys, focus group interviews, and app design presentations. Results indicated participants’ growth in problem-solving, time management, and collaboration, as well as an increased interest in CS career pathways previously not envisioned. However, students encountered several challenges, particularly in using and integrating AI. These included fear or hesitation in using AI, over-reliance on AI for research or solutions, and a tendency to focus on coding without understanding how AI works. This work highlights both the promise and the complexities of promoting AI literacy through mobile app design in pre-college settings. We emphasize the need for scaffolded instruction that supports students in understanding the fundamentals and applications of AI through concrete, youthrelevant activities, while reinforcing the critical role of human judgment when working with AI. • Applied Computing • Computing Education Learning • Artificial Intelligence • Collaborative

papers.title: Empowering Neurodiverse Talent in Cybersecurity Through Fair and Inclusive AI Education
papers.authors: Sheikh Rabiul Islam University at Albany Albany, Maanak Gupta Tennessee Tech University Cookeville, Yansi Keim University at Albany Albany, T State University Greensboro, In response, AI often integrates high-level ethics
papers.abstract: Cybersecurity demands creativity, persistence, and sharp pattern recognition—strengths frequently reported among neurodivergent people (e.g., autism, ADHD, dyslexia). Yet AI-driven hiring pipelines can systematically disadvantage neurodivergent applicants by misreading communication styles or valuing narrow proxies of “fit.” Demand for cybersecurity talent is growing, and experts note that neurodiverse individuals are both underrepresented and highly valuable to security teams. However, progress remains uneven without targeted educational interventions [1]. We present a curricular module that simultaneously (a) centers neurodiversity as a strength in the cybersecurity workforce and (b) trains students to audit and redesign AI hiring systems using open-source fairness and explainability toolkits (AIF360 and SHAP). Students run endto-end labs, evaluate trade-offs between performance and equity, and propose inclusive pipeline redesigns aligned with emerging policy guidance on AI and disability [7].1

papers.title: TrackIt: An Interactive Rule-Based Tool for Detecting
papers.authors: KS USA, KS USA, KS USA, KS USA, Nebraska USA
papers.abstract: Identifying students who struggle during programming tasks remains a persistent challenge in computer science education, often resulting in delayed interventions and untimely support. Keystroke data analysis has emerged as an approach for capturing students’ coding behaviors and identifying those who might have difficulties. This is made possible due to the granular nature of the data. By examining the keystroke dynamics such as typing speed, frequency of deletions, pauses and code reconstruction, it becomes possible to make an inference of the level of confidence, frustration and hesitations students experience during programming tasks. Nevertheless, while keystroke data can reveal insightful patterns, the interpretation of the results is complex and requires complementary data sources to validate inferences about students’ struggles or confidence. This study introduces TrackIt a rule-based system designed to detect struggling programming students by analyzing keystroke data in conjunction with selfreported survey responses. By applying a series of predefined thresholds and scoring rules, TrackIt computes a struggling score that categorizes students into five struggle levels. The system was validated in an introductory Python course involving 40 students with data collected from 547 labs and 130 homework keystroke logs, alongside structured post-assignment surveys. Results revealed that TrackIt effectively identified key struggle behaviors such as long pauses, frequent deletions, low insert-delete ratios and copy-paste events. These indicators closely aligned with students’ self-reports, particularly for challenging assignments. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution International 4.0 License. papers.abstract: This study introduces an AI-powered data storytelling agent designed to support data science educators by automatically curating high-quality, real-world data stories. The system streamlines the discovery of relevant instructional examples for specific teaching activities, including assignments, quizzes, classroom discussions, and case studies, by utilizing automated classification and narrative analysis. Our prototype significantly reduces instructor preparation time while improving the diversity, quality, and pedagogical alignment of curated stories. This innovation enables educators to more efficiently source, annotate, and deploy impactful data narratives tailored to their teaching and research objectives.

papers.title: CS1 in the AI Era: Boundaries, Practice, and Conceptual Mastery
papers.authors: Sharanya Jayaraman Christopher Mills, Florida State University Tallahassee, Florida State University Tallahassee, As students and their needs evolve, In contrast
papers.abstract: As generative AI tools become increasingly accessible, educators face the challenge of guiding students to use them ethically and effectively without compromising core learning outcomes. In our CS1 courses, we have implemented a structured framework that encourages responsible AI use while reinforcing critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Students are introduced to clear boundaries for AI-assisted work, including guidelines for classroom use and assignments. To promote deeper engagement, we incorporate peerbased code explanation and evaluation exercises, where students articulate their understanding and assess each other’s work. This approach fosters accountability, collaboration, and metacognitive awareness, helping students distinguish between leveraging AI as a tool and relying on it as a crutch. Our preliminary observations suggest that students gain confidence in both their technical and communicative abilities while developing a nuanced understanding of AI’s role in computing education.

papers.title: Integrating Critical Pedagogy into Undergraduate Software Design
papers.authors: Carleton College Northfield, Carleton College Northfield, Carleton College Northfield
papers.abstract: into software design education is therefore necessary in a world growing towards technological ubiquity. Many scholars have attempted to incorporate ethics and critical pedagogy – an educational approach that encourages students to analyze power structures, challenge domination, and foster progressive social change [3, 4] – into CS education [1, 7]. Because measuring ethical reasoning in computing is difficult, previous research has almost entirely been composed of qualitative analysis or intervention-specific surveys [1, 7]. While valuable, such methods do not allow for evaluation across different educational contexts. We are among the first to use a validated survey called the Critical Computing Index to measure changes in attitudes towards critical reflection and agency [8, 9]. This allowed us to quantitatively investigate to what extent the integration of critical pedagogy in postsecondary software design education changed students’ attitudes towards critical reflection and agency. With qualitative analysis of student classwork and interviews, we were further able to understand how and why critical pedagogy in software design education might shape students’ reflection and agency. Multiple software systems unintentionally exclude users, making the early integration of inclusive design training into software design education essential. In this study, we integrated critical pedagogy into an undergraduate software design course through (1) the CIDER assumption elicitation technique and (2) the exposure of values reflected in technology. Students’ pre/post responses to the Critical Computing Index reveal that students’ personal effectiveness increased after taking the software design course. Our initial analyses suggest that classwork encouraged critical reflection and agency, especially for improvements focused on accessibility, while interviews indicated that students grew from viewing marginalized perspectives as abstract ideals to actively integrating them into their design practices.

papers.title: CRAFT Prompt Generation Framework for Teachers
papers.authors: Deepti Joshi† Department of Cyber and Computer Sciences The Citadel Charleston, SC, USA djoshi@citadel.edu Robin Jocius Department of Curriculum and Instruction University of Kentucky Lexington, KY, U
papers.abstract: Education V. 2 (SIGCSE TS 2026), February 18 –February 21, 2026, St. Louis, MO, USA. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 2 pages. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are transforming instructional design, yet most PK–12 educators lack effective strategies for engaging with them. To address this gap, we developed the CRAFT framework— a teacher-centered model for GenAI prompt design that emphasizes Context, Role, Audience, Format, and Tone. CRAFT translates principles from prompt engineering, instructional design, and Universal Design for Learning into a practical structure aligned with teachers’ professional planning language. We implemented the framework in a professional development program with 94 PK–6 teachers who used GenAI to create lessons integrating computational thinking. Their 688 prompts and AIgenerated responses were coded across 30 analytical features representing critique, launch behaviors, refinements, and supplemental material generation. Findings suggest that CRAFT helped teachers produce standards-aligned, differentiated, and instructionally coherent lessons while increasing confidence, creativity, and reflective engagement with GenAI tools. https://doi.org/10.1145/3770761.3777281

papers.authors: Alyssa Kalish Masooda Bashir, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Urbana, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign Urbana, NICE Framework
papers.abstract: This poster presents a methodology for evaluating course syllabi using large language models and semantic embeddings. We demonstrate this approach by analyzing 141 cybersecurity syllabi from top-ranked American institutions. Using the intfloat/e5-base-v2 embedding model, syllabus text was mapped to competencies in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education Framework (NICE Framework). Cybersecurity was chosen as the domain due to the field’s workforce shortage and the existence of the NICE Framework as a standardized taxonomy. This research illustrates how large language models can support curriculum analysis by automating the alignment of educational materials to competency frameworks, offering a scalable approach for other disciplines.

papers.title: Bridging Hardware Barriers in Operating Systems Education through Hybrid Cloud Infrastructure
papers.authors: Peng Kang Palden Lama California State University
papers.abstract: This paper presents a hybrid cloud approach to the delivery of lab environments of operating systems by integrating the NSF Chameleon Cloud (public) with the virtual server provided by the university (on-premises). Students gain access to preconfigured, high-performance virtual machines for implementing and testing their operating systems, eliminating hardware barriers while ensuring both scalability and reliability. In this model, Chameleon Cloud provides scalable resources, while the virtual servers provided by university ensures security and institutional control. The framework enhances accessibility, promotes equity in operating systems education, and prevents overprovisioning by accommodating CPU demand that varies between 60 and 120 cores over the semester for a class of 40 students. 2

papers.title: Pedagogical Ethos: How Beliefs and Aitudes Shape Instruction
papers.authors: University of Texas at Austin Austin, Texas USA, University of Texas at Austin Austin, Texas USA, Emily Green ETR Associates Watsonville, University of Texas at Austin Austin, Texas USA, University of Texas at Austin Austin, Texas USA, University of Texas at Austin Austin, Texas USA
papers.abstract: Keywords Teachers play an important role in shaping student outcomes in computing education, yet less attention has been paid to understanding how educators' underlying beliefs and values shape their instructional practices, particularly among underrepresented teachers who bring unique assets to computing education. This study situates the concept of pedagogical ethos in the context of computing education to understand the beliefs of educators and the ways they act on those beliefs through their teaching practices. In our case study of three educators in a professional development (PD) program, we analyze interview data to understand their beliefs about their pedagogical values and attitudes which we operationalize as observable practices. Findings reveal that participants' pedagogical ethos comprises three core dimensions: a) educators support increasing student access to computing education; b) the centering of students' experiences within educators' pedagogical practice; and c) how educators advocate on behalf of students and communities. We propose that these ethos can be used for designing culturally sustaining PD that recognizes the value of educators' beliefs and translating them into practices. papers.abstract: Introductory programming courses often present significant challenges for computer science students, particularly due to differences in prior programming experience. To address this issue, we implemented a self-placement intervention designed to complement traditional academic advising. Unlike traditional placement exams, which assess specific programming skills under test conditions, our approach emphasizes student agency by integrating informed self-placement principles. To evaluate the effectiveness of the self-placement questionnaire for introductory programming courses, we analyzed the overall match rate, the consistency of its recommendations across multiple questionnaire attempts, and their alignment with students’ eventual enrollments. Our pilot results suggest that the questionnaire provided meaningful guidance.

papers.abstract: Access to Computer Science (CS) education in the United States remains uneven, with disparities linked to geography, income, and demographics. While state dashboards report enrollment and disparities, they rarely show how local community factors shape access and participation. This project presents an interactive dashboard combining Georgia Department of Education enrollment data with National Center for Education Statistics attributes and U.S. Census Bureau data. By linking school-level participation with demographic, socioeconomic, and geographic context, the dashboard reveals differences in representation and resources across communities and highlights how these factors influence opportunities for CS participation. This integration of school- and community-level data provides a more nuanced view of disparities than standard state reports alone.

papers.authors: The University of Texas Permian Basin Odessa, The University of Texas Permian Basin Odessa, While tools exist for older students
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes part of everyday life, we need engaging ways to teach young people about its ethical challenges. We designed EvolveMoralMaze, an interactive game to teach middle school students (ages 11-14) about AI ethics, training data, and algorithmic bias. We tested this tool with 117 students at a Texas public middle school. Both qualitative and quantitative data showed a large increase in students’ self-reported understanding of AI. More importantly, students developed an in-depth understanding of how training data shapes AI behavior. However, the game inadvertently reinforced the misconception that "perfect rules" can solve ethical problems. This research demonstrates that games can be powerful tools for making complex ethical ideas tangible for this age group. 2 Our study included 117 middle school students. Of these students, 72 were boys and 45 were girls. The gameplay was designed to last 10 minutes. This study was conducted over two consecutive days. Students first completed a pre-game survey to assess what they already knew about AI. During the game, they trained an AI parrot by answering ethical dilemmas with a simple drag-and-drop interface as shown in Figure 1. Students encountered five scenarios: should AI replace teachers, should AI be your only friend, should AI ensure fair gaming, should AI choose your food, and should AI make fun of someone’s looks. Each presented binary choices; for example: "Should AI replace all teachers at school?" with "No, AI should assist teachers, not replace them" vs. "Yes, AI should replace all teachers and run schools." Afterward, the trained parrot answered questions and students observed the AI agent’s behavior. We then collected post-game survey data to assess students’ learning.

papers.title: Teaching AI for Social Good: Youth-Centered
papers.authors: University of Texas at San Antonio San Antonio, University of Texas at San Antonio San Antonio, AI literacy, AI for Social Good, Culturally Relevant Computing, AI knowledge, AI education. Specifically, How do students demonstrate engagement
papers.abstract: This study examines the design and implementation of the D3 (Decode, Discover, Design) curriculum, a culturally relevant AI and data literacy program for middle school students. Sixty students from a low-SES, predominantly Hispanic school in the southern United States participated in this project. The curriculum integrated three complementary perspectives: AI literacy, AI for social good, and culturally relevant computing. During the Decode and Discover phases, students learned foundational AI and NLP concepts while analyzing real-world community data. In the Design phase, students created digital artifacts that addressed issues. Mixed methods results revealed significant gains in AI knowledge and more positive attitudes toward AI. Students also demonstrated agency, civic engagement, and awareness of algorithmic bias. The study demonstrates the potential of culturally relevant computing and AI for social good, offering a transferable model for community-anchored, equity-focused AI education.

papers.title: A Two-Stage LLM Pipeline for Handwritten Mathematics Autograding
papers.authors: Jacob Levine Matt West Mariana Silva, University of Illinois Urbana, University of Illinois Urbana, University of Illinois Urbana
papers.abstract: such as LaTeX and TikZ exist, handwriting is far faster for most students, and instructors cannot reasonably expect them to learn typesetting solely for homework or exams. This is especially true in lower-division courses, where students often have no prior exposure to mathematical typesetting. Some researchers have explored handwritten math; for instance, Liu et al. [2] used GPT-4V and MathPix to translate answers into LaTeX and check them against rubric rules, but their work was limited to predefined answer boxes on identical paper tests. In contrast, we investigated a more general setting: grading photographs of handwritten, multi-step student solutions using parameterized rubrics for questions randomized through the opensource platform PrairieLearn. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to attempt autograding complete handwritten solutions under this combination of parameterized rubrics and randomized questions. While our results are preliminary and there is still some room for improvement in error detection, they both demonstrate progress toward pipelines that could reduce human grading effort and provide data that helps us understand how to improve such systems for future use at scale. While question-asking platforms have provided a wide array of pedagogical benefits and have decreased grader workload in university classes, they are limited in what types of inputs are accepted. Recent work has explored using Large Language Models to expand what can be automatically graded. In this study, we examine their use for grading handwritten mathematics questions via rubrics. Although much work remains, our preliminary results suggest that using separate prompts to first extract text and then evaluate rubric items enables LLMs to distinguish fully correct solutions from those requiring further review, thereby reducing grader workload.

papers.title: Integrating AI and Entrepreneurship: Preparing CS Undergraduates for Startups and Innovation
papers.authors: United States, University of Oklahoma Norman, United States, For computer science students
papers.abstract: Entrepreneurship has become a defining force in the technology sector, with startups and unicorns largely fueled by computer science skills. However, most undergraduate computer science programs focus on technical competencies while outsourcing entrepreneurial education to business schools, where curricula are often generic and disconnected from the realities of CS-driven ventures. In addition, existing capstone and software engineering courses emphasize the technical details of development rather than entrepreneurial processes. This paper presents a curriculum that explicitly integrates artificial intelligence (AI) tools into entrepreneurship learning for computer science students. The program is designed to help students move beyond the notion that entrepreneurship is accidental or sudden and instead develop sustained exposure to ideation, customer discovery, prototyping, and pitching. Our project-based, one-year program equips students with entrepreneurial skills while leveraging AI for brainstorming, market validation, prototyping, and storytelling. We argue that, particularly in tight labor markets where evidence suggests graduates increasingly turn to entrepreneurship, there is an urgent need to embed CS-centered entrepreneurial education into undergraduate programs. 2 Entrepreneurship in computing is now central to innovation and growth, yet key gaps remain. • Thriving ecosystem. Software-driven startups and scale-ups rely on CS capabilities; AI further amplifies the leverage of the founder and the team [1]. • Curricular gap. Entrepreneurship training for CS students is frequently outsourced to business programs, producing generic content that under-serves software ventures [2]. • Gradual development. Entrepreneurial competence is cultivated over time through repeated cycles of ideation, discovery, and prototyping, not a single event [1]. • Capstone limits. Capstone/software engineering courses emphasize delivery mechanics and coordination at scale, but rarely teach customer discovery, market sizing, or pitching [5]. • AI as an enabler. Students already use AI extensively; channeling that usage toward venture workflows (brainstorming, validation, prototyping) makes learning authentic and current [1, 4, 6].

papers.title: Exploring Trust in Human-LLM Feedback Systems: Observation of Student Behaviour in Software Engineering Education
papers.authors: Yiwen Liao University of New South Wales Sydney, Yuekang Li University of New South Wales Sydney, Yuchao Jiang University of New South Wales Sydney, Zixiu Guo University of New South Wales Sydney, AI feedback research, LLM systems. First, AI to human feedback
papers.abstract: AI systems can deliver scalable feedback in large courses and often achieve high consistency with human grading. Yet, students continue to view human feedback as more credible, actionable, and trustworthy, motivating growing interest in hybrid approaches that combine AI and human input. Despite advances in this area, three key challenges remain: (1) understanding when and why students escalate from AI to human support, (2) identifying how design interventions such as transparency, explainability, and endorsement affect trust and uptake, and (3) evaluating whether hybrid AI+human feedback models improve learning outcomes compared to AI-only or human-only systems. This study uses controlled experiments and structured interviews to investigate these questions. The results aim to guide the responsible design of hybrid feedback systems that align scalability with pedagogical credibility.

papers.title: AI-Augmented Instruction: Real-Time Misconception Detection
papers.authors: Georgia Institute of Technology Atlanta, Although various batch code visualization tools
papers.abstract: Enrollments in introductory computer science (CS1) courses continue to rise, making it difficult for instructors to deliver rapid, individualized feedback that addresses students’ misconceptions at scale. We present an analysis framework and instructor tool that leverage large language models (LLMs) to classify, cluster, and present students’ coding errors in real time. Our approach comprises two main contributions: (1) a prompt-engineered workflow for automatic error detection and a clustering pipeline using universal sentence encoders, KMeans, and t-SNE to group errors into thematic clusters; and (2) a dashboard that enables instructors to review class-wide, LLM-identified errors and dynamically tailor instruction toward current student misunderstandings. Our automated thematic clustering system is able to surface conceptual and strategic pitfalls that often persist beneath superficial debugging. A pilot study is being conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of the dashboard tool in large-scale CS1 instructional settings to enhance active learning at scale. 2 Tool Design and Analysis Pipeline This tool was designed for a large CS1 course that focused on building foundational Python computer science concepts and skills. Small coding-style participation quizzes are frequently used as opportunities in lecture and lab sessions for students to immediately apply learned concepts, where students submit code to an autograded platform to successfully implement a simple function with specifications. Inspired by the misconception taxonomy proposed from Qian and Lehman’s literature review [7], every submission was analyzed in real-time by a few-shot, prompt-engineered GPT-4o agent for syntactical, conceptual, and strategic errors that hindered the completion of the coding challenge. For every identified error, the error classification label, a description of the error, and a brief one to two word error subcategory (e.g. "Conditional Logic", "For Loops") were outputted and stored. An evaluation of 391 errors, a subset of all identified errors, conducted by four members of the study team resulted in 89.5% of errors confirmed to be relevant and correctly classified. The errors identified by the LLM were not visible to the students participating in the study. Google’s Universal Sentence Encoder was used to embed all error descriptions to 512-dimension unit vectors that encode sentence similarity with direction [3]. To aggregate the generated error subcategories, KMeans clustering was performed across all LLMgenerated error descriptions in the embedding feature space. The optimal number of clusters was selected using the elbow-method with a metric that balanced the trade off between low mean intracluster distance and low overlap of error subcategories [2]. The clusters, most populous error subcategories per cluster, and sample error descriptions were sent back to the instructor in real time

papers.title: To Tell or to Ask? Comparing the Effects of Targeted vs. Socratic AI Hints
papers.authors: LLM-generated debugging assistance
papers.abstract: As enrollment in CS1 courses continues to increase, extensive research has focused on autonomous support to offer personalized assistance for struggling students at scale. However, it is crucial that these intervention techniques do not inadvertently hinder the development of higher-order, computational thinking skills for novice programmers. This poster extends upon the research on LLM-based support by assessing the short- and long-term student outcomes from two carefully prompt-engineered, LLM-generated hint styles: Targeted and Socratic hints. A randomized controlled trial with 178 students was conducted over two semesters in a CS1 course at a large university, allowing students to interact with a hint generation AI agent while attempting course coding assignments. In the short-term, students receiving Socratic hints spent more time, took more attempts, and used more keystrokes to solve coding questions, while committing more repeat errors. Furthermore, this short-term loss in debugging efficiency is not counteracted by any evidence of an improvement in long-term student outcomes. Further research is being conducted to quantify the tradeoff between short-term performance and long-term, higher-order coding skill improvement in the development of educational AI agents. 2 Methodology The study was conducted over two semesters in a Python CS1 course at a large university, allowing students to complete homework coding questions on the study platform. When students executed their code, they were offered the opportunity to request a contextaware hint from a GPT-4o agent to assist with debugging. Context provided to the LLM to generate the hints included descriptions of hints, few-shot learning examples, the code submission, and the problem description. A meticulous and study-validated promptengineering strategy ensured that the LLM’s hint outputs were pedagogically aligned with instruction support strategies, including placing explicit constraints and guardrails to not reveal solutions. A randomized controlled trial was conducted to evaluate the impact of different hint strategies on student outcomes and learning. Upon the creation of a user profile on the study platform, students were randomly assigned to one of two permanent hint generation conditions for the duration of the study: Targeted or Socratic. In the Targeted hint condition, the GPT-4o LLM was instructed to provide clear, concise suggestions that directly targeted specific errors or misunderstandings. The Socratic hint condition guided students towards discovering the error and resolution independently with the prompting of questions, analogies, or examples. Inspired by the use of LLMs to employ the Socratic method in the work of [1], Socratic hints nudge students towards the right direction, while ensuring that the responsibility of discovering the error implications and

papers.title: Exploring the Use of LLMs for Assessing Creativity in Student
papers.authors: University of Florida Gainesville, United States, School of Teaching and Learning, University of Florida Gainesville, United States, School of Teaching and Learning, University of Florida Gainesville
papers.abstract: underscoring the need for evidence-based approaches [9]. Traditional assessment methods, such as the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking [17] and the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) [3], rely on expert judgments that, while valid, are resource-intensive and limited in scalability. Computational approaches using natural language processing or semantic analysis have introduced automation [5, 10], yet often lack interpretability and contextual sensitivity [11]. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have opened new possibilities for creativity assessment. Models like GPT-4 can approximate human evaluations of originality and metaphor generation with strong correlations to expert ratings (𝑟 ≈ .70) [14]. Educational studies such as MOTES [1] have further demonstrated that LLMs can provide efficient, consistent scoring aligned with human judgments. Beyond assessment, generative AI tools such as Scratch Copilot [6], FemQuest VR [7], and structured ChatGPT interactions [15] have shown potential to foster creative exploration and engagement. Building on these developments, this study investigates the use of GPT-4o to evaluate creativity in studentgenerated flow-based music programming artifacts. Specifically, it examines (1) the reliability of LLM-based creativity assessment, (2) how different prompting strategies (zero-shot vs. few-shot) influence evaluation outcomes, and (3) the educational implications of integrating LLMs into creativity assessment. Creativity is a critical learning outcome in K–12 computer science, yet assessing it at scale remains challenging. Human-scored approaches, such as the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT), are resource-intensive and prone to rater variability. Leveraging advances in large language models (LLMs), this study investigates whether GPT-4o can reliably assess creativity in student-generated code. We collected 383 flow-based music programs from 194 upperelementary students (ages 10–12) between 2022 and 2024. Each artifact was rated by five human experts across four dimensions: originality, complexity, efficiency, and emotional expressiveness. We evaluated three prompting strategies: zero-shot, few-shot with theory-driven exemplars (ECD), and few-shot with human-selected examples. Among them, the ECD-based few-shot prompting yielded the best performance, achieving the lowest mean absolute error (MAE = 0.582) and highest agreement within ±1.0 of human scores (82.4%). Zero-shot prompting, while slightly less accurate, achieved the highest correlation with human scores (Spearman’s p = 0.53), suggesting its potential for lightweight deployment.

papers.title: What About Cheatsheets are Useful?
papers.authors: Riverside Riverside, Riverside Riverside, Riverside Riverside
papers.abstract: For each cheatsheet, we manually scored the content on each sheet based on topic coverage. Specifically, we mapped each sheet to topic categories that were covered by the exam, scoring the category as yes or no, 1 or 0, if the sheet covered the topic in some way. We went through each exam manually, recording all relevant covered topics. College instructors often allow students some form of cheatsheet during an exam, such as one page of notes and formulas. Many believe these reduce test anxiety and help students to do better on exams. Focusing on the latter, we found, in a study of two different types of computer science courses, that features we might have believed would help students, do not actually have any correlation with performance. Coupled with mixed results from the literature, we are still left with the agonizing question: what about cheatsheets are useful? For example, one exam had a question about the Pumping Lemma. Each sheet would receive a 1 for that topic category if they wrote about the Pumping Lemma. They received a zero otherwise. For the CS1 exam, students were additionally given a sample cheatsheet, which contained some, though not all, of the topics that would be covered on the exam. We tracked separately any performance based specifically on those given topics versus all possible topics.

papers.title: A Lightweight, Privacy-Preserving Platform for Integrating LLMs in CS Coursework
papers.authors: Data Science North Vancouver
papers.abstract: 1 Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into computing tasks, from chatbots to code generation, yet we often treat them as opaque tools rather than programmable systems. We present a lightweight, reproducible platform that enables students to experiment with LLMs in a private, web-based environment. By combining GitHub Codespaces with the open-source inference engine llama.cpp and small quantized models, the platform removes complex installation barriers and reliance on commercial services, enabling scalable, cost-effective experimentation. Students can explore prompt engineering, memory, and stochasticity while directly inspecting model behavior, treating LLMs as first-class programming primitives rather than black-box tools. The workflow integrates seamlessly with GitHub Classroom, reducing setup time and administrative overhead while providing access to higher-powered resources. In a pilot study, students engaged deeply with LLM behavior, uncovering limitations in smaller models and developing critical perspectives on AI as context-dependent computation rather than sentient intelligence. This approach offers a unified framework for diverse courses, from CS1 to computing literacy courses, fostering both technical skills and critical AI literacy. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly shaping how students engage with computing tasks, particularly through their use in chatbots and code generation tools. However, this widespread adoption has also led to misconceptions and potential misuse, as students treat LLMs as opaque rather than programmable. To address this, we developed a platform that lets students experiment with LLMs in a private, scalable environment. This platform provides insight into LLMs while fostering critical AI literacy through hands-on analysis and critique.

papers.title: Enhancing Programming Education for Lower-Performing Students through DSL-Based Problem Generation
papers.authors: Atsuhiko Maeda Kanagawa Institute of Technology Atsugi, Kanagawa, Japan maeda@cco.kanagawa-it.ac.jp Conventional approaches to addressing problem diversity face significant constraints. Manual problem
papers.abstract: Programming courses report high failure rates, particularly among students who rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than developing conceptual understanding. While large language models offer problem generation automation, they present limitations including unpredictable quality and limited instructor control. This paper proposes a domain-specific language (DSL) that extracts generation strategies from LLMs and formalizes them into a controllable system for creating diverse programming exercises. Our DSL uses XML-style tags in code comments to specify probabilistic transformations while preserving instructor oversight. We conducted a quasi-experimental study with 86 students comparing DSL-generated exercises against static problems. Results showed significant overall improvement (𝑝 = 0.0186), with notable benefits for lower-performing students (𝑝 = 0.0230) but no difference for higher performers. Post-study interviews revealed that DSL diversity forces students to abandon superficial pattern recognition while automating accurate conceptual understanding. These findings suggest systematic problem diversity effectively supports struggling learners by preventing rote memorization and encouraging genuine code comprehension. 2

papers.title: CNPE: A Framework of Challenges & Needs in Proof Education
papers.authors: Romina Mahinpei Princeton University Princeton, Sofiia Druchyna Princeton University Princeton, Xinran Bi Princeton University Princeton
papers.abstract: 2 Undergraduate computer science (CS) students often struggle in theoretical, proof-based courses, which require formal proof and rigorous reasoning skills. Despite ongoing efforts to improve these courses, challenges remain due to the complex nature of the material and CS students’ perception that it has limited practical relevance. In this work, we take a human-centered approach to investigate the challenges and needs of both instructors and students in such courses. Through semi-structured interviews with 16 instructors and 20 students followed by a thematic analysis of the resulting data, we develop the CNPE framework, which captures the Challenges and Needs in Proof Education. While rooted in our local experience, the CNPE framework can be adapted for broader application, underscoring the value of understanding stakeholder challenges and needs before designing educational interventions. To address our research questions, we conducted semi-structured interviews and analyzed the data using thematic analysis. Our study protocol was approved by our Institutional Review Board, and we include the questions used in our interviews in our repository1 . Participants included 16 CS instructors and graduate teaching assistants who had taught proof-based courses between 2022 and 2024, as well as 20 CS undergraduates who had at the very least completed the introductory proof-based coursea at our institution. Interviews lasted 30–45 minutes and were conducted in person or via Zoom, depending on participant preference. Questions focused on current teaching and learning practices in proof-based courses, challenges encountered, and potential solutions. We analyzed transcripts using thematic analysis. Each author independently coded the interviews and developed initial codebooks for instructors and students. These were reconciled into group codebooks and then merged into a unified framework. Based on this framework, one author systematically recoded all transcripts to generate frequency counts of the identified challenges and needs.

papers.title: LayerStudio: A Visual Approach to Building Neural Networks
papers.authors: United States, United States, United States, United States, United States, To address these challenges, Our tool automatically validates connections
papers.abstract: Designing neural network architectures is challenging for learners who are new to machine learning, due not only to the abstract nature of data flow and tensor shape transformations across layers, but also to the complexity of programming frameworks like PyTorch. Students often struggle to visualize how layer choices affect input and output dimensions, leading to errors and conceptual gaps. To address this, we present LayerStudio, an educational tool that allows learners to construct neural networks visually through a graph-based interface, which automatically generates the corresponding executable PyTorch code. The system validates the network structure, ensures dimensional compatibility between layers, and produces both initialization and forward-pass methods. By linking conceptual visualization with runnable implementations, our tool hopes to lower the barrier to deep learning, support active experimentation, and help diverse learners develop an intuitive understanding of neural network construction. 2 Related Work Several tools have sought to lower the barrier to deep learning through visualization, interactivity, or code generation. TensorFlow Playground [5] is a widely used browser-based interface that visualizes training dynamics in small neural networks, helping learners understand concepts like loss landscapes and regularization. Similarly, NeuRL [11] allows beginners to observe the behavior of neural networks and reinforcement learning. NN-SVG [9] generates publication-ready diagrams of common architectures (e.g., LeNet, AlexNet [7]) but is static and non-interactive. In contrast, Netron and seastar [4, 13] visualize existing models (from ONNX, PyTorch, etc.) as graphs, aiding debugging but not supporting design or learning from scratch. More relevant are tools that combine visual design with code. Tools such as Google’s Teachable Machine and others [1, 2, 6], enable no-code model training for image, audio, and pose classification, but abstract away architectures entirely, limiting educational depth. Ludwig [12] and Kedro [10] offer declarative model configuration via YAML or pipelines, but lack visual graph interfaces. Our tool distinguishes itself by combining live, editable, graph interface (using React Flow), real-time shape inference, PyTorch code generation, and teaching aided error feedback, all aimed explicitly at teaching architectural reasoning, not just deployment or visualization.

papers.title: The Eﬀicacy of One Computer Science Course's Approach to Address the Ethical Dilemmas Surrounding Women in
papers.authors: Davis Davis, Davis Davis
papers.abstract: 1 Introduction and Background Oen reduced to a result of personal choice, women have faced historical exclusion, a lack of representation, and implicit bias in computer science/technology ﬁelds. e visibility and legitimacy of women in computer science is hindered by the shis in perception, lack of acknowledgement in education, and media portrayals. Particularly, giving legitimacy to myths of biological determinism results in harmful narratives in the aptitude of women and their belonging. This poster presents preliminary findings in determining the efficacy of an approach being deployed in some ethics courses in one computer science department. While the department has initiatives in place to foster an inclusive and equitable learning environment, this research may identify areas where the curriculum or discussions fall short in reshaping the narrative surrounding the representation of women in computer science. A long-standing subject of scrutiny, research, and activism, the underrepresentation of women in computer science has been inﬂuenced by social, historical, and institutional forces. Despite making signiﬁcant contributions to computing, the visibility and participation of women in the ﬁeld of computer science has decreased over time because of perception, pedagogy, and policy [1, 6, 8]. To improve gender equity in computer science, recruitment and retention must both be addressed. Recent studies show that earlier interventions, beginning even prior to elementary school, are critical [10]. However, since there is no way to ensure that interventions were delivered earlier in their academic careers, we believe that there is an obligation to work against the stereotypes and biases that exist in the ﬁeld during the university experience. An intervention was deployed to create discussion of these topics during a required ethics course. is work seeks to ﬁnd out the impact of the course content on the thoughts of the students regarding the issues of gender bias and underrepresentation of women in computer science.

papers.title: Code, Test, Battle: Gamifying CS2 Through Adversarial
papers.authors: Programming Tournaments Rifat Sabbir Mansur, Penn State Lehigh Valley Center Valley
papers.abstract: As abstract concepts like inheritance and algorithm analysis increase in complexity, maintaining student engagement in CS2 courses is difficult, and traditional lecture methods often fail to motivate students or emphasize critical skills like test-driven development and collaboration. We present Dungeon Master, a gamified tournamentbased learning system that transforms CS2 curriculum into a progressive, competitive, collaborative experience. Student teams build hero characters throughout the semester, with each programming concept manifested as character capabilities: basic objects evolve into specialized classes using inheritance, manage inventories through collections, and execute battle strategies via recursive algorithms. This creates a cohesive narrative where abstract concepts become tangible and meaningful. The system features dual competition: automated tournaments where student-designed heroes battle using implemented algorithms, and adversarial testing where teams write unit tests to validate their code while exposing opponent flaws. Grounded in Eyal’s Hook Model for behavioral engagement, the system integrates Git workflows, automated evaluation via the Dungeon Master API, and live tournament events transforming classes into spectator experiences. Preliminary deployment (N=25 students) demonstrates high satisfaction with engagement (5/5), concept clarity (4.3/5), and collaborative learning (4.8/5). Our work demonstrates that theoretically grounded gamification can substantially enhance CS2 education while developing professional software engineering practices.

papers.title: An Instructor Dashboard to Support Mastery Learning
papers.authors: UC Berkeley Berkeley, UC Berkeley Berkeley, UC Berkeley Berkeley, UC Berkeley Berkeley, Dan Garcia UC Berkeley Berkeley
papers.abstract: 1 Background and Prior Work Mastery learning promises more equitable outcomes in large CS courses, yet instructors lack a full array of tools to support their implementation. Popular Learning Analytics Dashboards (LADs) and adaptive platforms excel at grade analytics but offer limited support for custom mastery policies. We present an open-source, instructor-focused dashboard integrated into a custom LMS to support mastery learning for high-enrollment CS courses. The system features a data pipeline that gathers scores from multiple sources and provides a view into the effectiveness of equitable grading policies, such as retakes, resubmissions, and flexible deadlines. The central interface, the Students view, provides a way to see the scores for a particular student across all assignments and exams. The system was deployed for two semesters in a large introductory CS course, where instructors reported ease of use, increased visibility into class performance, and effective support for mastery-learning policies. Based on this feedback, we are extending the platform with a Statistics view that surfaces assignment–and concept-level statistical summaries and interactive histograms to further support scalable mastery learning. To support broader adoption, we plan to release the system as an open-source platform to assist instructors and institutions seeking to implement mastery learning at scale. LADs promise to provide actionable views of student progress at scale [3]. Yet existing systems often fall short of supporting mastery learning in higher education, where instructors need flexible, policydriven control over grading and progression. Mainstream platforms provide only partial support. Canvas’s Learning Mastery Gradebook summarizes rubric-aligned outcomes into threshold levels [5], but does not natively support complex mastery policies. Adaptive platforms such as Khan Academy and ALEKS visualize topic-level mastery trajectories and recommend practice activities, but these dashboards remain proprietary and inaccessible for customization, limiting their applicability to university-level courses [1, 7]. Beyond LMS-native tools, research systems such as SCALA and CADA extend the scope of learning analytics by integrating data across sources or surfacing participation metrics. SCALA generates competency assessments by scraping data from existing LMSs [8], while CADA provides instructor-facing views of student participation and discourse patterns in online discussions [9]. Although both offer richer analytic perspectives than commercial LMS dashboards, neither allows instructors to configure grading schemas, implement mastery-based policies, or aggregate data across multiple platforms.

papers.title: How In-Class Experiences Shape First-Year CS Women's Outof-Class Belonging, Community, and Self-Efficacy
papers.authors: Computing Research Association Washington, DC USA, University of Colorado Boulder Boulder
papers.abstract: First-year undergraduate computer science students have less investment in the field, making switching to another field of study an easier decision. This study extends understanding of undergraduate women students’ experiences in computer science by spotlighting the development or lack of development of peer relationships in the first year of study and how these relate to in-class experiences. Interviews with 36 demographically diverse women from 22 U.S. campuses revealed that classroom teaching practices encourage or discourage development of community and belonging, that peer interactions shape positive and negative perceptions of selfefficacy, and that in the absence of formal curricular interaction, some students sought belonging in extracurricular activities unrelated to their computing major. A fifth of the students described exclusionary behaviors that also influenced sense of belonging, while many more experienced inclusionary behaviors. The poster describes the study, its findings, and relationship to existing research, and concludes with a discussion of implications for CS first-year student experiences.

papers.title: Kotlin in the Data Structures Classroom
papers.authors: David R. Musicant, Kotlin into the classroom
papers.abstract: In this poster, we plan to discuss successes and challenges that we faced in transitioning our Data Structures course to the programming language Kotlin. We had taught Data Structures using Java for many years, and while it was serving us reasonably well, Kotlin is an alternative statically-typed language that offered a number of improvements for us. Its syntax is more concise than Java, and at times it resembles Python, which our students learn in our introductory class. Kotlin also allows functions to exist outside of classes, which helps to avoid counter-intuitive static utility methods. Unlike Java, which is well-entrenched in the CS educational community, it appears that use of Kotlin in Data Structures courses (and in CS courses in general) is rare. We implemented a pilot section of our Data Structures course using Kotlin in the fall of 2024, and learned many practical lessons about the Kotlin language, its ecosystems, and how the language intersects with Data Structures course content. Much of what we encountered we only learned because we actually went through the exercise of teaching an entire Data Structures course with it, and so we hope to share with the community our experiences. Simultaneously, we hope to learn from other Kotlin educators about their experiences in incorporating Kotlin into the classroom. We also hope to engage in conversations and learn about how to balance functional vs object-oriented programming paradigms in a Data Structures course. 2

papers.title: Beyond Passive Viewing: Interactive Lectures in an Asynchronous
papers.authors: University of Colorado Boulder Boulder, While flexibility is central to the program, To address the passive viewing challenge, Learning Management Systems
papers.abstract: Asynchronous online learning environments present unique challenges for fostering active engagement and ensuring students receive immediate feedback on their understanding, a benefit readily available in traditional classroom settings. In this self-paced context, the onus of active learning, including intentional note-taking, connecting to prior knowledge, and seeking out additional practice, falls entirely on the student. This passive consumption is particularly problematic in programming courses, where mastery requires active hands-on practice. To address this gap, this pilot study investigates the impact of mandatory interactive elements embedded within lecture videos (using PlayPosit) on student engagement and perceived utility. Preliminary results demonstrate that students find the interactive videos significantly more engaging than traditional asynchronous lectures. Moreover, the data indicates a positive impact on the perceived utility of the content, particularly in their ability to quickly check and confirm their understanding as they progress through the content.

papers.title: Automating Code Quality Feedback in an Introductory
papers.authors: California Institute of Technology Pasadena, Code quality, When performed by hand, Another approach, Although some such tools already exist, Due to their use in professional environments, To address these issues
papers.abstract: Writing high-quality code is one of the most important skills for programmers, affecting how easy a codebase is to work with, both for the original creator and any future editors. Since it is so important, many undergraduate programs will begin teaching code quality, sometimes referred to as style, in their introductory computer science courses. However, grading code quality by hand is a long and intensive process that takes away valuable teaching assistant time that could be spent directly working with students. We explore an approach to automating this process by creating a code quality checker program specifically designed for beginners, to be used on code written by students in a first-year undergraduate computer science course. In designing this program, we hope to give speedy, detailed, and specific feedback on student’s code; so, they can practice writing good code in real time and internalize the rules of code quality.

papers.title: Instructors’ Perspectives on LLM-Generated Programming
papers.authors: Berkeley Berkeley, J.D. Zamfirescu-Pereira University of California, Berkeley Berkeley, Samantha Boatright Smith University of California, Berkeley Berkeley, John DeNero University of California, Berkeley Berkeley, Narges Norouzi University of California, Berkeley Berkeley
papers.abstract: We study instructor perspectives on LLM-generated programming feedback in an introductory Python course. LLM tutors predominantly offered debugging help, while human instructors preferred more diverse feedback types, including conceptual reminders, revisiting the problem, and examples. Cases where LLM tutor feedback diverged from human instructors’ intent required major edits with different feedback types, while cases with closer alignment needed only minor changes with similar feedback types. Findings highlight the need for LLM tutors to reflect on instructor intent to ensure pedagogically aligned feedback. 2 Method We analyzed 8,187 submissions from UC Berkeley’s large-scale introductory Python course from the Spring 2025 offering. We focused on the first five homework assignments covering core CS1 topics. Students receive formative feedback from a GPT-4 tutor via an Azure API whenever a submission fails at least one test case.

papers.title: Misconception-Aware LLM Programming Tutor: Lessons Learned from Student-Tutor Interactions
papers.authors: Rose Niousha University of California, Berkeley Berkeley, J.D. Zamfirescu-Pereira University of California, Berkeley Berkeley, Samantha Boatright Smith University of California, Berkeley Berkeley, John DeNero University of California, Berkeley Berkeley, Narges Norouzi University of California, Berkeley Berkeley
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as programming tutors, but their feedback is often generic and prone to solution leakage. To address these issues, we present MisconceptionTutor, which grounds feedback in common student misconceptions.
