papers.title: “Born Accessible” Visualizers for Scheme Program State
papers.authors: Jacob Bell, Grinnell College Grinnell, USA Salyan Karki, Grinnell College Grinnell, USA William Pitchford, Grinnell College Grinnell, USA Anna Deschamps Eva Kapoor, Grinnell College Grinnell, Grinnell College Grinnell, Grinnell College Grinnell, USA Elene Sturua, Grinnell College Grinnell
papers.abstract: morenoni@grinnell.edu Grinnell College Grinnell, IA, USA Charles Wade wadechar@grinnell.edu Grinnell College Grinnell, IA, USA “Born Accessible” Visualizers for Scheme Program State. In Proceedings of the 57th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V.2 (SIGCSE TS 2026), February 18–21, 2026, St. Louis, MO, USA. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 2 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3770761.3777157 Students in introductory classes often struggle to understand why the programs they write behave as they do. Increasingly, faculty find that by helping students develop mental models of the program state, they build an infrastructure that aids students in developing, interpreting, and debugging their own code and grounds explanations of new aspects of the language. Tools such as Python Tutor have demonstrations the value of providing students with a visual model of program state, showing a simplified version of the contents of the stack and the heap. Unfortunately, many of these visualizations are inaccessible or have limited utility to blind and low-vision learners. This lack provides the opportunity to create new descriptive tools as we build visual models for Scheme. In this paper, we describe our design and implementation of an accessible visualizer for the state of Scheme programs, particularly representing Scheme structures such as lists, pairs, vectors, and structs. We consider how to provide appropriate navigation for substructures and the approaches we use to narrate/describe each component. 1 Problem and Motivation Many introductory computer science students struggle to understand the behavior of their programs. Confusion arises for a variety of reasons. However, one of the most common is a reported inability to conceptualize the state of their programs and how their variables and data structures are manipulated at run time. More recently, instructors have found that providing and fostering a “mental model” of the program state, and by proxy visualizations of state elements, students perform better [11]. These mental models are crucial in allowing students to develop, interpret, and debug their code while also laying a strong foundation for understanding new aspects of the language [7]. In this project, we are designing a program state visualization system for Scamper [8], a pedagogical IDE for a dialect of Scheme. Because it is important to include accessibility early, rather than as a subsequent “add-on” [9, 12], our design emphasizes navigation support and sonification for students who are blind or have low vision (BLV), as they stand to gain the least from visual models that lack appropriate support.

papers.title: Improving Privilege Levels and Memory Protection for Teaching in Embedded Xinu
papers.authors: Marquette University Milwaukee, Marquette University Milwaukee
papers.abstract: 1.2 The RISC-V computer architecture has generated a lot of interest within computer science communities and has seen increased usage in recent years with companies like NVIDIA, Huawei, and Google having announced or begun to produce hardware incorporating the RISC-V architecture. Because of this popularity, Embedded Xinu, a simple, education focused operating system, was ported to RISC-V. While Embedded Xinu successfully ran on RISC-V, due to limitations in RISC-V boot loader technology, the kernel was required to break privilege level specifications and configure the hardware directly from machine mode. To remedy this, the kernel and boot sequence needed modifications to run exclusively in supervisor mode, as intended in the RISC-V specifications. These modifications allow for proper hands on instruction regarding privilege levels and userkernel space distinctions, improving the breadth and quality of operating systems education using Embedded Xinu. 1.2.1 Xinu History. Embedded Xinu is based on the Xinu operating system developed by Douglas Comer [6] in the 1980s. In the late 2000s Xinu was ported to the MIPS32 architecture under the new name “Embedded Xinu”, as part of an experimental lab for teaching operating systems on baremetal hardware [3]. Embedded Xinu is designed to be lightweight and architecture agnostic, allowing it to be ported to numerous architectures and hardwares. In 2013 Embedded Xinu was ported to ARM64 on the newly popularized Raspberry Pi platform [2], this platform was chosen for its low cost and flexible application. Embedded Xinu has been used as a research platform for educational improvements in a wide variety of undergraduate and graduate coursework [1, 4, 5, 9–11]. Background & Related Work 1.2.2 Embedded Xinu on RISC-V. The most recent port to RISC-V from ARM [7] was completed a few years ago and has successfully implemented both the basic feature set required for coursework, and more advanced, implementation specific features such as paging and virtualization. While this initial port was a great leap forward for Embedded Xinu, some important libraries such as “pthread” and the network stack are still under development. Additionally, some quirks of the Nezha hardware platform were left unresolved. The RISC-V port greatly simplified assignments in the associated operating systems course, allowing students to focus less on the implementation minutia, and more on the important concepts at hand. Paging, for example, was improved as the RISC-V hierarchical page tables have consistent size, allowing for page-table walks to be assigned to students for the first time.

papers.title: Pedagogical Process Models of Undergraduate Computing Tutors
papers.authors: Esse Ciego, Engineering University of Florida Gainesville, USA Skyler Steiert, Engineering University of Florida Gainesville, USA Amanpreet Kapoor
papers.abstract: 2 With growing enrollment in computing, undergraduate teaching assistants (UTAs) play a key role in managing large courses and supporting student learning. Yet, little is known about how UTAs actually teach students. To address this gap, we conducted an ethnographically informed study of seven UTAs at a large public university, observing 37.5 hours of office-hour interactions and conducting three hours of interviews. Our analysis identified six core pedagogical practices: asking open-ended questions, hands-on demonstrating, prompting, referencing resources, explaining, and expressing affect. We use these practices to build a pedagogical model, showing how UTAs adapt in real time to balance efficiency and student independence. Our work can inform UTA training and advance CSEd research by providing a framework for pedagogical decision-making. Prior research on pedagogical practices in CSEd has centered on instructors and instructional design rather than UTAs, as seen in work on active learning [11] and debugging [12]. In the limited research on UTAs, researchers have found a mismatch between their reported and observed practices. In interview studies, tutors describe encouraging independent learning through guiding questions and conceptual explanations [10], while some even report not touching a student’s keyboard to maintain this autonomy [6, 10]. However, observational studies show that tutors commonly fix students’ code by reading off their own solution [5], and these tutors often do not help with debugging [4]. This difference may stem from tutors’ reluctance to admit discouraged strategies when interviewed by CS instructors. Our work addresses this methodological gap by using ethnography informed observations to examine both UTAs’ pedagogical practices and their reasoning behind them.

papers.title: Impact of Computing Education by School Type and County on K-12 Students’ AI Literacy
papers.authors: University of Maryland College Park College Park, United States of America
papers.abstract: Introducing computational thinking to K-12 students generally relies on the availability of computer science (CS) classes and varies by school type and location. This study focuses on how location and the type(s) of school(s) students attend may impact their access to CS education and their resulting AI literacy. 20242025 AI literacy survey and focus group interview responses provided by students and CS curricula of schools are analyzed. ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey tests were performed to compare AI literacy levels of students attending different types of schools. ANOVA tests revealed that school type and county were significant at the p < 0.1 cutoff for the 2025 sample. Focus group findings revealed that students may not be receiving CS education as stated by their schools. 2 Background And Related Work AI literacy is a multidimensional construct encompassing AI knowledge, skills, ethics, and attitudes, including fundamentals, technological elements, and real-world applications [8]. Studies have demonstrated the positive impact of structured AI education. Targeted instruction can enhance students’ understanding of AI principles and improve the quality of their interactions with AI [1,7]. Middle school is identified as a critical intervention point where students are cognitively prepared to begin developing AI competency through structured, accessible learning experiences. Computational thinking (CT) is a foundational element of AI literacy, enabling students to reason algorithmically and interact with AI. Kandlhofer et al. [6] propose a model in which students progress from hands-on CS activities in early grades to advanced AI topics and programming challenges in high school. Visual programming languages are also entry points to computing, which later transition into more complex coding environments [2]. Despite these approaches, systemic barriers continue to hinder access to CT learning. There are inconsistencies in curriculum design and assessment standards [3,8], significant variation in curricular offerings across states and school types [5], and insufficient teacher training [2,6]. Equity concerns are prevalent: underfunded schools lack access to AI tools, exacerbating disparities in student exposure based on their school type [9]. This directly impacts students’ readiness to engage with AI concepts, especially in schools with limited resources or outdated curricula. Previous research suggests that school type and geographic location play a pivotal role in shaping students’ access to CS and CT education and their resulting AI literacy. The current study builds on these insights by examining how these factors influence students’ experiences using a mixed-methods approach to analyze both statistical trends and student perspectives.

papers.title: Adaptable Metrics to Assess and Improve Introductory CS
papers.authors: Harvey Mudd College Claremont, Harvey Mudd College Claremont
papers.abstract: (2) a terminal_game, with turn-taking and student-written AI (3) a text_classifier, with provided and invented features (4) a game_of_life of multiple rulesets and their statistics (5) a genetic_alg that itself evolves new programs Static code-analysis metrics have long been used to assess and guide successful software projects. Traditionally, these metrics have measured software’s commercial or professional suitability. This work explores six code metrics designed to provide educational insight, specifically comparing pre- and post-LLM student work. We measure over a thousand CS1 and CS2 projects, completed from 2018 to 2024. The results show a clear LLM-correlated impact on students’ early computing work, both positive and negative. We add perspective by tracking how the metrics vary across final-project themes. Our results underscore the enduring importance of curriculum, pedagogy, and scaffolding on student work. We conclude with our program’s ongoing adaptations to this mix of signals, increasing student agency and prioritizing student demonstrations and discussions of their chosen project work. This work shows how students’ software-creation experience differs across these project themes. We also track how the incorporation of LLMs has affected students’ project software. All of these assessments prompt improvements – and we conclude by sharing some of those ongoing efforts. This work asks the question, “What can different CS1 project types say about the student-computing relationship?” LLMs have changed the trajectory of computational skill-building, e.g., [4]. LLMs or not, all CS instructors track over time their choice of content, pedagogy, and philosophy. Code metrics are one such tracking method. By updating and adapting decades of thought vis-a-vis traditional software metrics, this work proposes – and demonstrates – the insights available using pedagogical metrics, as instantiated on the past seven years of introductory CS capstone projects.

papers.title: Investigating the Efficacy of Mastery-Based Tests in Fostering
papers.authors: Grinnell College Grinnell, USA Michael W. Asher, Carnegie Mellon University Pittsburgh, As a result, Mastery-Based Tests
papers.abstract: Given the cumulative nature of computer science, success in introductory computing (CS1) courses requires students to not only learn the material but also develop effective self-regulated learning (SRL) habits. While theories of SRL emphasize planning, performance, and self-reflection as essential phases of effective learning, there is limited evidence on how to help learners put these phases into practice. In this context, Mastery-Based Tests (MBT), which allow students to retake assessments after receiving feedback, have shown promise for improving learning outcomes. However, prior work in computer science is largely observational and does not directly test MBT’s impact on SRL behaviors. This paper presents a pilot study (N = 6) exploring this relationship in CS1. Using a between-subjects design, we observed that learners who first completed an MBT achieved higher post-test scores, demonstrated higher metacognitive accuracy, and self-reported more productive SRL behaviors. These patterns suggest that MBTs warrant further investigation as a viable scaffold for fostering self-regulation in CS1. • RQ1 How do mastery-based tests reshape students’ selfregulated learning behaviors in CS1 courses? • RQ2 Do these changes in self-regulated learning behavior lead to improved learning outcomes?

papers.title: Label-Free Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation in a University Policy Chatbot
papers.authors: Lusine Hayrapetyan California State University, San Bernardino San Bernardino, Evaluation must therefore rely on automated, This motivates the need for automated
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a common approach for building chatbots that combine fluent language generation with access to domain-specific knowledge. However, these systems often produce answers that are plausible but weakly supported by retrieved documents or that cite irrelevant sources. Evaluating RAG chatbots is difficult because it requires measuring both how well answers address user queries and how well they are grounded in retrieved content. University policy documents provide a useful test case. They are lengthy, formal, and regularly updated, yet they guide routine decisions for students and faculty. The combination of structured policies and varied user questions makes this domain well suited for systematic label-free evaluation. This study evaluates a RAG chatbot deployed at a large public university with over 700 pages of institutional policies. A dataset of 140 interaction logs was collected, and a refined subset was analyzed. Automated methods measured relevance (alignment of answers with questions), groundedness (alignment with retrieved text), and retrieval effectiveness (Recall@k and Mean Reciprocal Rank). Results show moderate performance on both relevance (0.64) and groundedness (0.66), with strong retrieval coverage but weaker ranking. Additional analyses examined how input clarity, phrasing style, and conversation behavior influenced chatbot performance. 2 Early chatbot evaluation often used overlap metrics such as BLEU or ROUGE [1]. These methods compare generated and reference answers, but they struggle when multiple phrasings can still be correct and they require labeled datasets that are not available for many real world chatbots. More recent work has used embeddings to measure semantic similarity. Sentence BERT and related models [2] allow comparisons between questions, answers, and retrieved passages in a way that better captures meaning. These approaches have been applied in areas such as biomedical question answering and tutoring systems, where labeled data is scarce [3]. Frameworks like RAGAs [4] extend this direction by combining several label free measures, including answer relevance, faithfulness, and context precision. Other research has investigated using large language models as judges [5], where models are prompted to evaluate or verify responses, although these methods can be costly and sensitive to prompt design. Despite this progress, few studies apply label free evaluation to real chatbot logs in domains like university policy. Most prior work relies on benchmarks or simulated datasets, which leaves open how well automated metrics capture performance when chatbots are used by actual students, faculty, and staff.

papers.title: Teacher Capacity as a Catalyst: Examining a Research-Practice Partnership’s Impact
papers.authors: Texas USA, CS teachers identify as White, CS course, Research-Practice Partnerships
papers.abstract: This study examines how eighteen teachers’ participation in a Texas-based Research-Practice Partnership (RPP) impacted their pedagogical capacity to shape students' access to, participation in, and experiences within computer science education (CSEd). Teachers engaged in comprehensive professional development (PD) that included content knowledge training, innovative pedagogy courses, and collaborative workshops. Data collection included semi-structured interviews collected after year two of teacher participation in the program, and interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis combining deductive coding based on the CAPE framework (Fletcher & Warner, 2021) with inductive analysis of emerging themes. Findings revealed that the RPP helped teachers expand conceptions of access beyond course availability to address systemic barriers through intentional recruitment and pipeline creation; developed specific strategies ensuring increased participation by monitoring classroom demographics and using varied participation methods; and created relevant experiences by integrating students' lived contexts and leveraging the participants own authentic identities as pedagogy. This research demonstrates how RPPs develop teachers' pedagogical capacity through sustained and relevant PD, revealing that PD translates into teaching practices with appropriate scaffolding and time, ultimately fostering learning environments where all students can thrive in CSEd. 2 Background and Related Work Fletcher and Warner's CAPE framework provides a systematic lens for examining equity throughout the CSEd ecosystem [6]. The framework comprises four progressive components: Capacity (resources to support high-quality CS instruction including faculty, funding, policies, certified teachers), Access (attending schools offering CS courses), Participation (actual enrollment when courses are offered), and Experience (learning outcomes, sense of belonging, culturally relevant curriculum). The framework has been widely adopted since 2021, and extensions by McGill et al. developed the Theory of Impacts-CAPE model for evaluating the impact of complex interventions (such as RPPs) through the CAPE lens [7]. RPPs offer a paradigm shift from traditional PD through sustained collaboration, co-design, and iterative improvement [9], yet we lack understanding of how these features develop teacher capacity to impact access, participation, and experience, particularly for minoritized teachers whose lived experiences and cultural assets can transform each CAPE component.

papers.title: Characterizing the Relationship Between Generative AI, Student Behavior, and Learning Outcomes in Upper-Level CS Education: A Case Study in an Undergraduate Machine Learning Course
papers.authors: Anha Khan, Princeton University Computer Science Princeton, New Jersey, USA Romina Mahinpei, Princeton University Computer Science Princeton, New Jersey, USA Victoria Dean Maryam Hedayati, Princeton University Computer Science Princeton, New Jersey, USA Ruth Fong, Princeton University Computer Science Princeton, New Jersey, Princeton University Computer Science Princeton, New Jersey
papers.abstract: 57th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V.2 (SIGCSE TS 2026), February 18–21, 2026, St. Louis, MO, USA. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 2 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3770761.3777156 As generative artificial intelligence (genAI) tools become embedded in computing education workflows, it is essential to understand how students use such systems to learn beyond introductory programming. This work investigates the relationship between the use of genAI by students and their conceptual understanding of mathematical and algorithmic principles in an undergraduate machine learning course with 134 students. We deploy a course-specific, custom-interfaced large language model (LLM), CubBot, to examine (1) how students interact with genAI in an upper-level CS course via an analysis of anonymized chat logs and (2) how genAI usage relates to students’ conceptual understanding and learning outcomes via a randomized, controlled assessment comparing performance with and without CubBot access. This research contributes to the growing body of work on genAI-supported education by providing one of the first empirical investigations into genAI’s relationship with conceptual learning in an upper-level CS course.

papers.title: Automated Assessment Tools: Feedback to and from Students
papers.authors: HE CS, HE CS courses. Our research questions
papers.abstract: We have developed a novel Automated Assessment Tool (AAT) facilitating formative assessments for novice programming students in a Higher Education (HE) CS setting. This AAT forms an analogue of traditional in-person HE CS computer lab sessions. Traditionally teaching staff would engage with students in-person offering feedback to, and receiving feedback from, students about learning materials. Meaningful two-way communication can be difficult to achieve with individuals in larger HE CS cohorts, which may be taught in a blended way. Our novel AAT offers automatically generated feedback to students and captures feedback from students (per question and per assessment) to inform teaching practice. The novel AAT has been used in four semesters with student volunteers from the authors HE CS setting. A mixed-methods approach has captured qualitative and quantitative data. Key findings are: 1. Parsons problem type questions were associated with no negative feedback from students in initial or repeat experiments, unique amongst the four AAT question-types available. 2. Students report concerns about providing free text feedback per question, but we observe this is a valuable source of information for teaching staff - if automatically collated for presentation in conjunction with other types of feedback from students and learning analytics. This research informs on best practices supporting communication between novice programming students and teaching staff where an AAT is a pedagogical necessity, promoting consideration for automatically collated student feedback, as part of AATs. Future work should replicate the experiments conducted in other HE CS settings.

papers.title: Undergraduate Students’ Struggles in Computer Science
papers.authors: Sai Neha Nakirikanti, Georgia Institute of Technology Atlanta, Georgia Institute of Technology Atlanta, USA Betsy DiSalvo, Georgia Institute of Technology Atlanta
papers.abstract: Computing Education Research (CER) has made valuable contributions to improving undergraduate computing. CER tends to focus on instructional challenges, developing tools and techniques for teaching, or researching a single institution or classroom experience, and as a result, may lack a student-first perspective. To identify if there were student concerns that current research was overlooking, we designed an open-ended survey that asked undergraduate computing students what struggles they experienced and how they solved or coped with those struggles. This paper reports on this survey with 𝑁 = 201 responses from 45 US institutions. Our analysis identified two primary factors in student concerns: social/personal and academic/structural. Many of the top concerns of students aligned with trends in CER literature; however, there were issues, particularly those related to structural factors (curriculum, lengthy content, lack of institutional support, and uninterested professors), that have little representation in CER literature. Many of these issues may have temporal context, suggesting ongoing data collection from students may help identify appropriate directions and trends for CER. While we know students struggle in many ways, this survey provides evidence that further research in areas that are pressing today may be under-addressed. 2 Related work A recent meta-analysis of CER literature identified a focus on CS pedagogy, with programming education as the most studied topic [5]. This meta-analysis suggests that there is a larger focus on pedagogy and assessment than on direct discussions with students about their educational experiences or institutional support/structure. It is also unclear if these topics are based on student need or instructors’ expectations/research interests in CER. While extensive research in CER has solicited student perspectives, these focus on student assessment [2, 3], with specific populations (e.g., women or underrepresented groups) [1, 6], or concern areas (e.g., identity or culturally relevant pedagogy) [4, 7]. These studies illustrate important areas for improvement in CER, but are reflective of researchers’ focus on subgroups or problems, and do not encompass the broader range of student struggles. To address the gap in CER we follow exploratory research practices through an open-ended survey that provides students with a platform to share their experiences. We focused our analysis on identifying common student struggles and the problem-solving strategies CS students use to determine whether these align with the literature and identify topics in need of a greater research focus.

papers.title: Teaching Middle School Learners AI Hallucinations Through
papers.authors: Chatbot Design Deniz Ozturk, North Carolina State University Raleigh, North Carolina, USA capabilities
papers.abstract: Equipping users with the ability to recognize AI hallucinations is essential for AI literacy. Building on research highlighting a lack of studies involving younger learners in the chatbot design process, we explore a constructionist approach to AI literacy focusing on understanding of hallucinations. We engaged 48 middle school learners in designing LLM-based chatbots with customized characters, roles, and constraints using a learning environment, LUMI. Through peer testing and collaborative evaluation, learners developed practical strategies for identifying hallucinations and understanding AI limitations. Pre- and post-surveys revealed substantial improvements in learners’ AI understanding, awareness of AI hallucinations, and confidence in designing trustworthy chatbots. Qualitative analysis showed that learners developed foundational understanding of chatbot functionality, LLMs, and prompt design, while demonstrating recognition of data limitations and strategies to mitigate hallucinations. This work contributes to teaching responsible AI interaction for youth learners. 2 AI hallucinations, where LLMs generate plausible but incorrect information [3], create particular challenge for young users who may overtrust these systems [1]. While detection tools exist [3], they target adult users rather than young learners. In K-12 AI education, frameworks emphasize understanding AI limitations [8], and chatbots serve as accessible entry points [7]. However, most educational chatbot tools do not involve learners in the design process [5], missing constructionist learning benefits where learners can develop knowledge through designing artifacts [4]. We address this gap by engaging learners in chatbot design and hallucination detection. Our goal is to provide both understanding of AI limitations and practical skills for responsible use to young learners.

papers.title: Ungraded Assignments in Introductory Computing: A Report
papers.authors: Yehya Sleiman Tellawi Abhishek K. Umrawal, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Urbana, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Urbana
papers.abstract: Ungraded assignments represent one such approach: they encourage engagement with course material without the pressure of formal assessment, allowing students to reflect, experiment, and take intellectual risks. Formats may include design exercises, optimization challenges, proofs, reflections, or multimedia tasks. Prior studies suggest that ungraded work can promote collaboration and deeper engagement [5], but most of this research has been situated in nontechnical fields. This gap motivates our investigation of ungraded assignments in a large introductory computer engineering course. Specifically, we examine how students engaged with optional ungraded tasks, how participation related to academic performance, and what assignment formats were most effective in fostering meaningful learning. We note that, unlike pedagogical ‘ungrading,’ our study focuses on optional tasks that are not included in the final course grade. This experience report explores the effects of ungraded assignments on the learning experience of students in an introductory computing course. Our study examines the impact of ungraded assignments on student engagement, understanding, and overall academic performance. We developed and administered new ungraded assignments for a required course in the first year of the Computer Engineering curriculum called ECE 120 Introduction to Computing. To assess the effectiveness of our ungraded assignments, we employed a mixed-methods approach, including surveys, interviews, and performance analysis. Our analysis shows a positive relationship between participation in ungraded assignments and overall course performance, suggesting these assignments may appeal to high-achieving students and/or support better outcomes.

papers.title: MerryQuery in the Loop:
papers.authors: North Carolina State University Raleigh, USA to close this gap by
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are increasingly woven into programming education, yet most studies are short-term and disconnected from coursework. To fill this gap, this work examines MerryQuery, a GenAI-powered assistant that grounds answers in instructorcurated materials, provides inline citations, offers scaffolded, stepby-step responses, and enables instructors to control response granularity and monitor student chat. MerryQuery was embedded across the weekly labs in an introductory MATLAB course, enrolling 313 non-CS majors. The mixed-methods analysis of the end-of-semester survey, and queries from representative early- and late-semester labs revealed that students had broadly positive perceptions and valued scaffolded guidance with citations, and queries were dominated by coding help. The study provides evidence of GenAI integration at scale, giving researchers and educators concrete insights for incorporating such tools into the classrooms. • RQ1. How do students perceive a course-integrated GenAIpowered assistant’s usefulness, design, and pedagogical value for supporting their learning? • RQ2. How does the type of student queries to the assistant evolve over the semester? 2 The widespread adoption of GenAI in programming education has largely been accompanied by positive student experiences and attitudes. Studies document increases in engagement and satisfaction [9], and learning outcomes and task completion rates [4]. Researchers have explored various pedagogical roles for AI assistants, from teaching assistants [2] to emotional supporters [5]. A growing body of work employs the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [3] to ground GenAI output in instructor-approved resources, showing an interest in curriculum-aligned content. Usagelog studies show that most queries are for coding help and debugging, with fewer inquiries focused on broader conceptual questions [7]. This study advances this landscape by designing a RAG-enabled assistant to integrate into an introductory programming course and providing a semester-long view of student queries and perceptions.

papers.title: Adaptive Uncertainty-Aware Fusion for Robust Multimodal Learning
papers.authors: Cy Xie Computer Science Department, De Anza College, CA USA
papers.abstract: ⚫ As single-modality models advance, multimodal learning systems are becoming critical for real-world deployments. However, their efficacy is consistently hindered by varying modality quality and reliability. Existing methods relying on uniform weighting or static correlation estimation fail to capture this dynamic landscape, leading to over-reliance on unreliable sources. ⚫ ⚫ We propose the Adaptive Uncertainty-Aware Fusion (AUAF) framework, which jointly models Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) via Monte Carlo Dropout and Cross-modal Consistency (CC) via latent-space cosine similarity. This enables principled, dynamic down-weighting of unreliable modalities. AUAF's decoupled architecture supports dual deployment: as a plug-and-play module or a fully integrated component within existing frameworks. Uncertainty Quantification (UQ): Leverages Monte Carlo Dropout to quantify uncertainty and down-weight unreliable modalities. Cross-Modal Consistency (CC): Uses cosine similarity to amplify coherent signals and expose representational discrepancies. Decoupled Modular Architecture: Operates independently of backbones, enabling flexible deployment as a plug-and-play monitor or trainable fusion layer without architectural constraints. 2 Background and Related Works Multimodal fusion has evolved from early and late fusion to sophisticated transformer-based architectures. While effective, these approaches have intrinsic limitations. Experiments on NLVR2 and selected portions of VQA v2.0 demonstrate that AUAF achieves superior performance and robustness compared to uniform weighting or correlation-based baselines, particularly with noisy or incomplete modalities. 2.1 Transformer-Based Architectures Transformer models like CLIP [1] revolutionize multimodal fusion through cross-attention mechanisms that learn joint representations. However, they assume stable modality quality and struggle with asymmetric reliability or noise.
